notations: GovernanceCompliant(Change)=True iff ApplicableRule and RequiredControls and Evidence

sources.note: Step 104: tests whether governance can actually control/constrain/explain/verify KnowledgeOS. Governance!=Documents; principle-vs-rule; scoped/temporal governance decisions and rule lifecycle; semantic-classification-over-Jira-label (directly reusing the real Softwareeinführungsprozess/ITCM classification dispute); WorkflowComplete!=GovernanceComplete; exception model with compensating controls; PolicyIntent vs PolicyControl and defense-in-depth enforcement; governance-to-code translation; the explicit non-automatable-decisions boundary and AI-recommendation-only classification role; governance versioning/drift/impact-analysis; the governance assurance loop as analogue of Step 100 architecture loop; governance-respecting DDD; governance ambiguity as first-class conflict knowledge becoming reusable once resolved; a GovernanceDecisionEngine that evaluates but never creates authority; and a 10-capability governance conformance matrix. Concludes KnowledgeOS=Semantic Model+Governance Model=Meaning+Authority.

rows.anchor: We now test the next architectural layer: Governance→KnowledgeOS. Can governance actually control, constrain, explain and verify what KnowledgeOS and its agents do? Target chain: Principle→Rule→Decision→Requirement→Implementation→Verification→Runtime. Feedback: Runtime→Evidence→Governance.
rows.statement: Frames Step 104's central test: whether governance can actually control/constrain/explain/verify KnowledgeOS, via Principle→Rule→Decision→Requirement→Implementation→Verification→Runtime with feedback Runtime→Evidence→Governance.

lineage_claims.quote: We now test the next architectural layer.

rows.anchor: 104.1 — Governance must have semantics ... The first mistake would be to equate Governance = Documents. A governance system needs at least Authority, Rule, Scope, Trigger, Decision, Responsibility, Evidence, Exception, Enforcement.
rows.statement: States Governance ≠ Documents; a real governance system requires Authority, Rule, Scope, Trigger, Decision, Responsibility, Evidence, Exception, Enforcement.

rows.anchor: 104.2 — Experiment 1: policy without authority ... KnowledgeOS contains a rule but cannot establish who owns it. Expected: GovernanceAuthority=Unknown. Therefore the statement cannot automatically be treated as authoritative governance. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a rule with no established owner has GovernanceAuthority=Unknown, so it cannot be treated as authoritative; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.3 — Principle versus rule ... A principle: 'production changes should be governed appropriately.' A rule: ProductionChange⇒RequiredGovernancePath. The latter is operationally testable.
rows.statement: Distinguishes an unenforceable Principle from an operationally testable Rule (ProductionChange⇒RequiredGovernancePath).

rows.anchor: 104.4 — Experiment 2 ... Architecture principle exists. No concrete decision rule exists. Expected: GovernanceIntent=True but ExecutableRule=False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2: a principle without a concrete rule is GovernanceIntent=True/ExecutableRule=False; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.5 — Governance decision ... 'Nexus upgrade requires architecture review.' KnowledgeOS should represent Decision+Authority+Scope+Validity.
rows.statement: States a governance decision must carry Decision+Authority+Scope+Validity, not just its content.

rows.anchor: 104.6 — Experiment 3 ... Architecture Board decides Nexus upgrade requires review, but no scope is recorded. Expected: ambiguity (Nexus only? all upgrades? all production software? all major versions?). Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: an unscoped board decision is ambiguous across multiple possible scopes; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.7 — Governance rule lifecycle ... Draft→Reviewed→Approved→Active→Superseded→Retired. This is consistent with the versioned knowledge model.
rows.statement: Defines the rule lifecycle Draft→Reviewed→Approved→Active→Superseded→Retired, consistent with versioned knowledge.

rows.anchor: 104.8 — Experiment 4 ... Old rule remains marked Active after a new rule supersedes it. Expected: governance conflict. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: an old rule still marked Active after supersession is a governance conflict; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.9 — Effective dates ... governance rules are temporal. Rule(t). A rule approved today may not have been valid yesterday.
rows.statement: States rules are temporal (Rule(t)): validity today does not imply validity yesterday.

rows.anchor: 104.10 — Experiment 5 ... A deployment occurred on 01.08. New governance rule became effective 15.08. Expected: the new rule must not automatically be applied retroactively unless explicitly defined. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: a rule effective 15.08 must not retroactively govern an 01.08 deployment absent explicit retroactivity; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.11 — Governance scope ... a rule can apply to Organization, Domain, Application, Environment, ChangeType.
rows.statement: Defines governance scope dimensions: Organization, Domain, Application, Environment, ChangeType.

rows.anchor: 104.12 — Experiment 6 ... Rule applies only to Production. Development deployment occurs. Expected: production rule does not automatically govern development. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: a production-scoped rule does not automatically govern a development deployment; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.13 — Trigger semantics ... NewSoftware, MaterialChange, ArchitectureImpact, SecurityImpact, ProductionDeployment. This directly connects to the Softwareeinführungsprozess / ITCM issue we have been working on.
rows.statement: Defines governance trigger types (NewSoftware/MaterialChange/ArchitectureImpact/SecurityImpact/ProductionDeployment), explicitly linked to the real Softwareeinführungsprozess/IT Change Management work in progress.

lineage_claims.quote: This directly connects to the Softwareeinführungsprozess / ITCM issue we have been working on.

rows.anchor: 104.14 — Experiment 7 ... A change occurs. Nobody knows whether it triggers Softwareeinführungsprozess or ITChangeManagement. Expected: governance ambiguity. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: not knowing which of two governance processes a change triggers is governance ambiguity; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.15 — Governance classification ... Change→Classification→GovernancePath. ArchitectureRelevant?, SecurityRelevant?, NewSoftware?, MaterialChange?
rows.statement: Defines a governance classification mechanism Change→Classification→GovernancePath, testing multiple classification questions.

rows.anchor: 104.16 — Experiment 8 ... Nexus version upgrade 3.69→3.70. System must determine whether this is normal change, software introduction, architecture-relevant, security-relevant, or major change. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: a version upgrade must be classified across multiple candidate governance categories; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.17 — Important principle ... KnowledgeOS should not merely ask what process does the Jira ticket say. It should ask what semantic change actually occurred. Then derive the governance implications.
rows.statement: States governance classification must derive from actual semantic change, not the informal Jira ticket label.

rows.anchor: 104.18 — Experiment 9 ... Ticket says 'routine maintenance.' Actual change introduces a new external dependency. Expected: semantic classification overrides an inaccurate informal label. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: a mislabeled 'routine maintenance' ticket that actually introduces a new dependency must be reclassified by semantic content, not the label; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.19 — Governance path ... Classification→RequiredSteps. ArchitectureImpact=True could require ArchitectureReview.
rows.statement: Defines Classification→RequiredSteps, e.g. ArchitectureImpact=True requiring ArchitectureReview.

rows.anchor: 104.20 — Experiment 10 ... Change is architecture-relevant. No architecture review is required by the system. Expected: governance enforcement gap. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: an architecture-relevant change with no required review is a governance enforcement gap; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.21 — Governance decision versus workflow status ... A Jira ticket may say Status=Done. That does not prove GovernanceApproved=True.
rows.statement: States workflow status (Done) does not prove governance approval.

rows.anchor: 104.22 — Experiment 11 ... Ticket Done. Architecture Board approval Missing. Expected: WorkflowComplete=True but GovernanceComplete=False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: a Done ticket lacking board approval is WorkflowComplete=True/GovernanceComplete=False; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.23 — Governance evidence ... a governance claim should be supported by DecisionRecord or ApprovalRecord. And that record should be linked to Authority.
rows.statement: Requires governance claims be supported by a DecisionRecord/ApprovalRecord linked to Authority.

rows.anchor: 104.24 — Experiment 12 ... System says 'architecture approved.' No approval record exists. Expected: UnsupportedGovernanceClaim. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: an unrecorded 'architecture approved' claim is UnsupportedGovernanceClaim; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.25 — Exceptions ... Real governance systems require exceptions. Rule: ArchitectureReviewRequired. Exception: EmergencyChange. But an exception must itself be governed.
rows.statement: Argues exceptions (e.g. EmergencyChange) are necessary but must themselves be governed.

rows.anchor: 104.26 — Exception model ... Exception=(Rule,Reason,Scope,Authority,Validity,CompensatingControls).
rows.statement: Defines Exception=(Rule,Reason,Scope,Authority,Validity,CompensatingControls).

type_signature.domain: Rule x Reason x Scope x Authority x Validity

rows.anchor: 104.27 — Experiment 13 ... Emergency change bypasses architecture review. No exception record exists. Expected: governance violation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: an unrecorded emergency-change exception is a governance violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.28 — Exception does not mean rule disappears ... Rule+AuthorizedException→PermittedDeviation. Not Rule→Ignored.
rows.statement: States Rule+AuthorizedException→PermittedDeviation, never Rule→Ignored.

rows.anchor: 104.29 — Experiment 14 ... Developer simply marks 'Emergency.' Expected: that label does not create a valid exception. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: a self-applied 'Emergency' label does not itself create a valid exception; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.30 — Compensating controls ... an exception may require CompensatingControl. EmergencyDeployment→PostDeploymentReview.
rows.statement: Defines compensating controls (e.g. EmergencyDeployment→PostDeploymentReview) as part of exception handling.

rows.anchor: 104.31 — Experiment 15 ... Emergency deployment occurs. No pre-review. But mandatory post-review is also missing. Expected: exception process incomplete. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: an emergency deployment missing its mandatory post-review compensating control is incomplete exception process; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.32 — Governance responsibility ... For every governance decision: ResponsibleRole. For every implementation: ResponsibleTeam. For every control: ControlOwner.
rows.statement: Defines required ownership roles: ResponsibleRole per decision, ResponsibleTeam per implementation, ControlOwner per control.

rows.anchor: 104.33 — Experiment 16 ... Architecture rule exists. Nobody owns maintaining the rule. Expected: governance lifecycle risk. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: an unowned architecture rule is a governance lifecycle risk; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.34 — Governance and KnowledgeOS ... GovernanceObject=(Rule,Authority,Scope,Lifecycle,Owner,Evidence,Enforcement).
rows.statement: Defines GovernanceObject=(Rule,Authority,Scope,Lifecycle,Owner,Evidence,Enforcement) as the KnowledgeOS governance model unit.

rows.anchor: 104.35 — The crucial test ... can KnowledgeOS answer why was this change allowed? Change→Classification→Rule→Decision→Authority→Evidence.
rows.statement: States the crucial explainability test: Change→Classification→Rule→Decision→Authority→Evidence answering 'why was this change allowed'.

rows.anchor: 104.36 — Experiment 17 ... Production change exists. KnowledgeOS can retrieve Decision and Approval. Expected: governance explanation is possible. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: retrieving Decision and Approval for a production change makes governance explanation possible; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.37 — Reverse question ... why was this change blocked? Change→PolicyViolation→BlockingRule.
rows.statement: Defines the reverse-explainability chain Change→PolicyViolation→BlockingRule for 'why was this blocked'.

rows.anchor: 104.38 — Experiment 18 ... Agent attempts unauthorized production modification. System blocks it. Expected: KnowledgeOS can explain WhichRule and WhichAuthority caused the block. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: a blocked unauthorized production modification must be explainable via WhichRule/WhichAuthority; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.39 — Governance must be enforceable ... A policy that nobody can enforce is PolicyIntent. An enforceable policy is PolicyControl.
rows.statement: Distinguishes unenforceable PolicyIntent from actually enforceable PolicyControl.

rows.anchor: 104.40 — Experiment 19 ... 'No direct production database modification.' But developers have unrestricted database credentials. Expected: policy is not technically enforced. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: a no-direct-modification rule undermined by unrestricted credentials is not technically enforced; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.41 — Enforcement layers ... HumanApproval, WorkflowGate, PolicyEngine, CI/CDGate, RuntimeAuthorization, NetworkControl. The strongest architecture uses multiple appropriate layers.
rows.statement: Lists six enforcement layers (HumanApproval, WorkflowGate, PolicyEngine, CI/CDGate, RuntimeAuthorization, NetworkControl), recommending multiple layers for strength.

rows.anchor: 104.42 — Experiment 20 ... CI prevents unauthorized deployment. But a developer can bypass CI and deploy directly. Expected: control is incomplete. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: a CI gate bypassable via direct deployment is incomplete control; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.43 — Defense in depth ... Governance→MultipleControls. This is especially important for Security and ProductionAuthority.
rows.statement: States defense-in-depth (multiple controls) is especially important for security and production authority governance.

rows.anchor: 104.44 — Governance-to-code ... GovernanceRule→MachineCheck. Rule: no unapproved production deployment. Machine check: Deployment.approved==True.
rows.statement: Defines the governance-to-code translation GovernanceRule→MachineCheck, e.g. Deployment.approved==True.

rows.anchor: 104.45 — Experiment 21 ... Governance rule exists. No automated enforcement exists. Expected: GovernanceAutomation=Incomplete. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: an unenforced-by-automation governance rule is GovernanceAutomation=Incomplete; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.46 — But not everything should be automated ... some decisions require human judgment, e.g. StrategicArchitectureDecision. KnowledgeOS should not pretend such decisions can be reduced entirely to boolean rules.
rows.statement: Warns strategic architecture decisions cannot be reduced entirely to boolean automated rules.

rows.anchor: 104.47 — Experiment 22 ... Architecture Board must choose between OptionA and OptionB with significant strategic trade-offs. Expected: AI can support the decision but does not replace authorized governance judgment. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: AI can support but not replace authorized governance judgment on a strategic trade-off decision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.48 — Human governance boundary ... KnowledgeOS ≠ GovernanceReplacement. Instead KnowledgeOS = GovernanceAugmentation+GovernanceExecution+GovernanceEvidence. Where appropriate.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS ≠ GovernanceReplacement; instead KnowledgeOS = GovernanceAugmentation+GovernanceExecution+GovernanceEvidence.

rows.anchor: 104.49 — Governance recommendation ... AI may generate Recommendation, e.g. 'this change appears architecture-relevant.' Then AuthorizedGovernanceActor→ClassificationDecision.
rows.statement: States AI produces classification Recommendation only; AuthorizedGovernanceActor makes the ClassificationDecision.

rows.anchor: 104.50 — Experiment 23 ... AI classifies a change as NonMaterial. Architecture Board disagrees. Expected: human governance decision can override the AI recommendation. Result: PASS. The override itself becomes evidence.
rows.statement: Experiment 23: a human board overriding an AI's NonMaterial classification is valid, and the override itself becomes evidence; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.51 — AI cannot silently change governance ... AIInference ⇏ GovernanceRuleChange. A governance rule changes only through its authorized lifecycle.
rows.statement: States AIInference ⇏ GovernanceRuleChange; rule changes require the authorized lifecycle.

rows.anchor: 104.52 — Experiment 24 ... Agent discovers a better governance rule. Expected: it may propose RuleChangeProposal. It cannot silently activate RuleChange. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: an agent's discovered rule improvement becomes RuleChangeProposal only, never silent RuleChange activation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.53 — Governance versioning ... if Rule_7→Rule_8, KnowledgeOS must know which rule governed each historical action.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS must track which rule version governed each historical action across rule transitions.

rows.anchor: 104.54 — Experiment 25 ... Deployment happened under Rule_7. Rule 8 becomes active later. Expected: historical deployment remains evaluated under Rule 7 unless retroactivity is explicitly defined. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: a deployment under Rule_7 remains evaluated under Rule_7 despite the later Rule_8 activation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.55 — Governance impact analysis ... changing a rule should identify AffectedProcesses, AffectedComponents, AffectedAgents, AffectedControls, AffectedEvidence.
rows.statement: Defines governance impact analysis identifying AffectedProcesses/Components/Agents/Controls/Evidence upon a rule change.

rows.anchor: 104.56 — Experiment 26 ... Change: AgentActionPolicy. Expected: KnowledgeOS identifies affected agent harnesses and authorization mechanisms. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 26: an AgentActionPolicy change must have its affected agent harnesses/authorization mechanisms identified; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.57 — This is where KnowledgeOS becomes extremely valuable ... Policy→DependencyGraph→AffectedSystems. That is executable governance intelligence.
rows.statement: States Policy→DependencyGraph→AffectedSystems as executable governance intelligence, replacing reliance on human memory.

rows.anchor: 104.58 — Governance drift ... ApprovedRule ⊭ Runtime. KnowledgeOS should detect GovernanceDrift.
rows.statement: Defines GovernanceDrift when ApprovedRule ⊭ Runtime (approved rule not reflected in actual runtime behavior).

rows.anchor: 104.59 — Experiment 27 ... Rule says all production changes require approval. Runtime observes an unapproved deployment. Expected: GovernanceViolation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: an unapproved production deployment despite the approval-required rule is GovernanceViolation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.60 — Governance assurance loop ... Rule→Control→Execution→Observation→Evidence→GovernanceAssurance. This is the governance equivalent of the architecture loop from Step 100.
rows.statement: Defines the governance assurance loop Rule→Control→Execution→Observation→Evidence→GovernanceAssurance, explicitly the governance analogue of Step 100's architecture closure loop.

lineage_claims.quote: This is the governance equivalent of the architecture loop from Step 100.

rows.anchor: 104.61 — Governance and architecture ... GovernanceRule→ArchitectureConstraint. 'ProductionChangeRequiresReview' becomes 'DeploymentGate.'
rows.statement: Defines the translation GovernanceRule→ArchitectureConstraint, e.g. ProductionChangeRequiresReview→DeploymentGate.

rows.anchor: 104.62 — Experiment 28 ... Governance rule exists but no architecture constraint derives from it. Expected: potential translation gap. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: a governance rule with no derived architecture constraint is a potential translation gap; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.63 — Governance and DDD ... SoftwareIntroduction may have a specific meaning in one process. MaterialChange another. We should not merge them merely because both trigger governance.
rows.statement: Applies DDD discipline to governance concepts: distinct trigger concepts (SoftwareIntroduction, MaterialChange) must not be merged as synonyms merely because both trigger governance.

rows.anchor: 104.64 — Experiment 29 ... 'Software Introduction' is used as a synonym for 'Change.' Expected: potential ubiquitous-language violation. Result: PASS. This directly relates to the governance ambiguity we identified previously.
rows.statement: Experiment 29: conflating 'Software Introduction' with 'Change' is a potential ubiquitous-language violation, directly tied to the previously identified real governance ambiguity; result PASS.

lineage_claims.quote: This directly relates to the governance ambiguity we identified previously.

rows.anchor: 104.65 — The governance decision point ... who determines the governance path? ClassificationEngine may recommend. ResponsibleRole may decide. ArchitectureBoard may decide for defined architectural matters. The exact organizational allocation must be explicitly established.
rows.statement: States the governance path decision authority (ClassificationEngine recommends, ResponsibleRole/ArchitectureBoard decides) must be explicitly and organizationally allocated, itself a governed question.

rows.anchor: 104.66 — Experiment 30 ... No role is defined as responsible for resolving governance classification ambiguity. Expected: GovernanceDecisionGap. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: an unassigned classification-ambiguity-resolution role is a GovernanceDecisionGap; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.67 — Governance ambiguity is itself knowledge ... if ProcessA and ProcessB both claim authority over a change, KnowledgeOS should record GovernanceConflict. Not arbitrarily choose one.
rows.statement: States competing process authority claims must be recorded as GovernanceConflict, never arbitrarily resolved.

rows.anchor: 104.68 — Experiment 31 ... Softwareeinführungsprozess and ITCM both classify the same event differently. Expected: GovernanceConflict until resolved. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 31: Softwareeinführungsprozess and ITCM disagreeing on classification of the same event is GovernanceConflict until resolved; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.69 — This is exactly our previous governance problem ... NewSoftware versus SoftwareChange. The deeper problem was not merely terminology. It was who determines the governance path? KnowledgeOS should eventually make this explicit.
rows.statement: Explicitly ties the model back to the real prior Nexus NewSoftware-vs-SoftwareChange dispute, reframing it as the deeper 'who determines the governance path' question KnowledgeOS should make explicit.

lineage_claims.quote: The Nexus discussion exposed a real-world version of this.

rows.anchor: 104.70 — Governance resolution ... Conflict→ArchitectureBoardDecision→RuleUpdate. Then the result becomes authoritative.
rows.statement: Defines the governance-conflict resolution chain Conflict→ArchitectureBoardDecision→RuleUpdate.

rows.anchor: 104.71 — Experiment 32 ... Board resolves: architecture-relevant changes follow the architecture governance path regardless of classification. Expected: decision becomes reusable governance knowledge. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 32: a board resolution becomes reusable governance knowledge, not a one-off decision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.72 — Governance as reusable knowledge ... A governance decision should not disappear into meeting minutes. Decision→Rule→ReusableKnowledge.
rows.statement: States governance decisions must become Decision→Rule→ReusableKnowledge, not disappear into meeting minutes.

rows.anchor: 104.73 — Experiment 33 ... Board makes the same classification decision three times. Expected: KnowledgeOS should surface the prior decision and avoid unnecessary reinvention. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 33: repeated identical classification decisions should be surfaced by KnowledgeOS to avoid reinvention; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.74 — Governance memory ... the system becomes organizational memory for Why, Who, When, UnderWhichRule, WithWhichEvidence.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS becomes organizational memory answering Why/Who/When/UnderWhichRule/WithWhichEvidence for governance.

rows.anchor: 104.75 — But memory must not become authority automatically ... a historical decision D_2025 may no longer be valid. HistoricalDecision ≠ CurrentRule.
rows.statement: States HistoricalDecision ≠ CurrentRule: a historical decision may no longer be valid and must not automatically be treated as current authority.

rows.anchor: 104.76 — Experiment 34 ... Old architecture decision is superseded. Agent retrieves it. Expected: agent sees Superseded. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 34: retrieving a superseded architecture decision must show it as Superseded; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.77 — Governance query capability ... a mature KnowledgeOS should answer what governance path applies to this change. Change→Context→Rules→Classification→GovernancePath.
rows.statement: Defines the full governance-query pipeline Change→Context→Rules→Classification→GovernancePath.

rows.anchor: 104.78 — Experiment 35 ... Input: 'upgrade Nexus from X to Y.' Expected output: applicable governance rules, classification, required approvals, affected architecture, evidence required, responsible authority. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 35: a governance query for a version upgrade must return applicable rules/classification/approvals/affected architecture/evidence/authority; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.79 — The governance engine ... GovernanceDecisionEngine whose responsibility is not to invent policy, but to apply approved governance semantics. Inputs: Change+Context+ApplicableRules. Outputs: Classification+RequiredControls+Authority+EvidenceRequirements.
rows.statement: Defines the GovernanceDecisionEngine as applying (not inventing) approved governance semantics, mapping Change+Context+ApplicableRules to Classification+RequiredControls+Authority+EvidenceRequirements.

type_signature.codomain: Classification x RequiredControls x Authority x EvidenceRequirements

rows.anchor: 104.80 — Important boundary ... The engine should not own the organization's authority. It evaluates ApprovedGovernance. It does not create Authority.
rows.statement: States the GovernanceDecisionEngine evaluates ApprovedGovernance but must never create Authority itself.

rows.anchor: 104.81 — Experiment 36 ... Governance engine receives no approved rule for a novel situation. Expected: Unknown/NeedsDecision. Not AutomaticallyApproved. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 36: a novel unruled situation must yield Unknown/NeedsDecision, never AutomaticallyApproved; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.82 — Governance escalation ... NoApplicableRule→Escalation. Similarly ConflictingRules→Escalation.
rows.statement: Defines escalation triggers NoApplicableRule→Escalation and ConflictingRules→Escalation.

rows.anchor: 104.83 — Experiment 37 ... Two active rules conflict. Expected: system does not silently select whichever appears first. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 37: conflicting active rules must never be resolved by silent first-match selection; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.84 — Governance assurance claim ... GovernanceCompliant(Change)=True only if ApplicableRule exists, RequiredControls were satisfied, and Evidence supports the claim.
rows.statement: Defines GovernanceCompliant(Change)=True as requiring an applicable rule, satisfied required controls, and supporting evidence.

rows.anchor: 104.85 — Experiment 38 ... Required approval missing. Expected: GovernanceCompliant=False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 38: a missing required approval yields GovernanceCompliant=False; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 104.86 — Governance conformance matrix ... Rule registry, Authority model, Change classification, Governance routing, Approval evidence, Exception handling, Policy enforcement, Governance drift, Versioning, Impact analysis -- each across Intended/Implemented/Enforced/Verified/Runtime, mostly marked
rows.statement: Presents a ten-capability governance conformance matrix (Intended/Implemented/Enforced/Verified/Runtime columns), designated as one of the central empirical artifacts, with most cells unresolved (?).

rows.anchor: 104.87 — New governance invariants: I_GovernanceAuthority, I_RuleLifecycle, I_GovernanceTraceability, I_ExceptionGovernance, I_GovernanceConflict, I_GovernanceFreshness, I_GovernanceEnforcement, I_AIGovernanceBoundary, I_GovernanceMemory
rows.statement: States nine new governance invariants: I_GovernanceAuthority (a governance decision must originate from an authority valid for its scope/time), I_RuleLifecycle (only rules in an authorized active state may govern current actions), I_GovernanceTraceability (material actions must be traceable to the governing rule/decision/pre-authorized policy), I_ExceptionGovernance (a deviation from a mandatory rule requires an explicitly authorized exception), I_GovernanceConflict (conflicting applicable governance rules must be surfaced, not silently resolved), I_GovernanceFreshness (superseded/expired rules must not silently govern current actions), I_GovernanceEnforcement (mandatory rules must have appropriate enforcement or explicit human control), I_AIGovernanceBoundary (AI recommendations/inferences must not silently become organizational authority), I_GovernanceMemory (material governance decisions must remain recoverable with authority/scope/rationale/validity).

rows.anchor: 104.88 — Step 104 verdict: STEP 104 — GOVERNANCE MODEL: PASS ... Again, this does not yet mean the existing KnowledgeOS implementation satisfies all these properties. It means we now have a precise conformance target. Does our actual implementation already contain this governance model?
rows.statement: Records Step 104 verdict PASS as a model-level target only, with the empirical question of actual implementation conformance left open.

rows.anchor: The major architectural result ... Steps 103 and 104 together establish KnowledgeOS = Semantic Model + Governance Model. The semantic model answers What is this? The governance model answers Who may decide or act on it, under which rules? Together: Meaning + Authority. That is the foundation require
rows.statement: States the combined result of Steps 103-104: KnowledgeOS = Semantic Model + Governance Model = Meaning + Authority, the foundation required before agents can safely participate.

rows.anchor: Step 105 — Agent Architecture Conformance ... Claude↔KnowledgeOS↔Codex. Are Claude and Codex actually agents operating against a shared governed knowledge system, or have we accidentally allowed each agent harness to become its own knowledge/governance system? We will specifically test AgentBehavior
rows.statement: Previews Step 105: testing whether Claude and Codex genuinely operate against a shared governed KnowledgeOS (Claude↔KnowledgeOS↔Codex) rather than each becoming its own knowledge/governance system, specifically re-testing AgentBehavior≠EngineeringKnowledge, AgentConfiguration→KnowledgeOS, and whether the .claude/ and .codex/ pointer-layer architecture is consistent with KnowledgeOS.

aliases: Collective Choice, Preference Aggregation and Legitimate Decision (Step 87)

sources.note: Step 87: formalizes collective/organizational decision-making distinct from mere preference aggregation. Covers Condorcet cycles, Arrows impossibility theorem, preference vs expertise vs authority vs evidence-quality as separate dimensions, weighted voting requiring weight provenance, quorum and veto as legitimacy/constraint mechanisms, delegation chains with temporal limits, human/AI authority asymmetry, strategic voting and agenda manipulation, evidence-weighted probability aggregation, decision-type-dependent aggregation rules, and the six-object hierarchy Truth->Belief->Preference->Recommendation->Decision->Authorization. Closely related to the pre-existing decision-power-model-lens (Recommendation/Decision separation) but adds the full collective-choice/voting-theory apparatus.

rows.anchor: Several legitimate agents may possess different knowledge, preferences, objectives, or authorities — yet the organization may still need to produce one decision ... How do we obtain D* without mathematically confusing majority preference with legitimate organizational decision?
rows.statement: Frames Step 87's central problem: how an organization derives one legitimate decision D* from multiple agents' differing knowledge/preferences/authority, without confusing majority preference with legitimate organizational decision.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 86 established that KnowledgeOS must account for strategic agents and mechanism design.

rows.anchor: 87.1 — Preference aggregation ... F(succ_1,...,succ_n)=succ*. The question is whether we can construct succ* while preserving desirable properties.
rows.statement: Defines a collective preference mechanism F(≻_1,...,≻_n)=≻* aggregating individual preference relations, asking whether desirable properties can be preserved.

rows.anchor: 87.2 — Experiment 1: simple majority ... A≻B, B≻C for two agents, third prefers C≻A. Pairwise majority produces a cycle. Expected: CollectivePreference may be non-transitive. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 1: pairwise-majority voting among three agents produces a cyclic collective preference (A≻B, B≻C, C≻A), demonstrating CollectivePreference may be non-transitive; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.3 — Condorcet cycle ... A≻B≻C≻A. There is no single alternative that defeats every other alternative. This is the classic difficulty of collective preference aggregation.
rows.statement: Names the resulting Condorcet cycle (A≻B≻C≻A) as the classic difficulty of collective preference aggregation, where no alternative defeats every other.

rows.anchor: 87.4 — Experiment 2 ... KnowledgeOS assumes MajorityPreference must always produce a consistent total ranking. Expected: False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2: the assumption that majority preference always yields a consistent total ranking is False; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.5 — Majority is not a universal solution ... Majority voting is a mechanism. It is not a mathematical law of collective rationality. MajorityDecision ≠ UniversalTruth.
rows.statement: States majority voting is a chosen mechanism, not a mathematical law of collective rationality: MajorityDecision ≠ UniversalTruth.

rows.anchor: 87.6 — Arrow's theorem ... no rank-order voting system can simultaneously satisfy a set of desirable conditions for unrestricted preferences with at least three alternatives. The KnowledgeOS lesson: there is no universally perfect preference aggregation mechanism. The organization must explicitly ch
rows.statement: States Arrow's impossibility theorem (no rank-order voting system can satisfy all classical desirable conditions with ≥3 alternatives) and draws the KnowledgeOS lesson that there is no universally perfect aggregation mechanism, so the organization must explicitly choose which properties to prioritize.

rows.anchor: 87.7 — Experiment 3 ... Organization demands simultaneously unrestricted preferences, non-dictatorship, Pareto consistency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, transitive collective ranking. Expected: mathematically impossible under classical Arrow framework. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: demanding simultaneously unrestricted preferences, non-dictatorship, Pareto consistency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and transitive ranking is mathematically impossible under the classical Arrow framework; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.8 — This changes governance design ... We cannot simply say 'KnowledgeOS will aggregate everyone's preferences correctly.' We must specify AggregationRule.
rows.statement: Concludes governance design must explicitly specify an AggregationRule rather than assume a generic 'correct aggregation' exists.

rows.anchor: 87.9 — Preference versus expertise ... Agent A may have Preference_A(A>B) while Agent B possesses substantially stronger evidence. Preference ≠ Expertise.
rows.statement: States Preference ≠ Expertise: an agent's stated preference is distinct from another agent's superior technical evidence/expertise.

rows.anchor: 87.10 — Experiment 4 ... Developer prefers A, security architect prefers B, evidence strongly indicates B reduces security risk. Simple majority selects A. Expected: Majority preference does not necessarily maximize technical correctness. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: simple majority selecting A (developer preference) over B (security-architect preference backed by stronger risk evidence) shows majority preference does not necessarily maximize technical correctness; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.11 — Epistemic versus preference aggregation ... Epistemic question: what is likely true? Value question: what do we prefer? Authority question: who may decide? These are three different dimensions.
rows.statement: Distinguishes three separate dimensions: the epistemic question (what is likely true), the value question (what do we prefer), and the authority question (who may decide).

rows.anchor: 87.12 — Experiment 5 ... Four engineers believe Risk=20. One security specialist has strong evidence Risk=80. System concludes Risk=20 because 4>1. Expected: EpistemicMajorityError. Result: PASS. The number of people holding a belief does not automatically determine its truth probability.
rows.statement: Experiment 5: concluding Risk=20 by majority count (4 vs 1) over a minority specialist's strong evidence (Risk=80) is EpistemicMajorityError; result PASS; belief headcount does not determine truth probability.

rows.anchor: 87.13 — Weighted voting ... Score(A)=Σ_i w_i v_i(A). But weights need justification. w_i could depend on formal authority, expertise, responsibility, jurisdiction.
rows.statement: Defines weighted-voting aggregation Score(A)=Σ w_i v_i(A), requiring weights w_i be justified by formal authority, expertise, responsibility, or jurisdiction rather than arbitrary.

rows.anchor: 87.14 — Experiment 6 ... w_security=5, w_developer=1. Expected: KnowledgeOS must preserve the semantic reason for those weights. Result: PASS. A weight without provenance is merely an arbitrary number.
rows.statement: Experiment 6: assigning w_security=5 vs w_developer=1 requires preserving the semantic justification for those weights; a weight without provenance is merely arbitrary; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.15 — Authority is not expertise ... An Architecture Board member may have Authority=High without being the strongest technical expert. Expertise=High does not necessarily imply DecisionAuthority=High.
rows.statement: States Authority ≠ Expertise: high formal authority does not imply top technical expertise, and vice versa.

rows.anchor: 87.16 — Experiment 7 ... Engineer has Expertise=High but Authority=0. Expected: engineer can provide evidence/recommendation but cannot independently authorize the decision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: an engineer with Expertise=High but Authority=0 can contribute evidence/recommendation but cannot independently authorize the decision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.17 — KnowledgeOS should therefore model at least: Expertise, EvidenceQuality, Preference, Authority separately.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS should model Expertise, EvidenceQuality, Preference, and Authority as separate dimensions.

rows.anchor: 87.18 — Experiment 8 ... System stores AgentWeight=0.8, no distinction between authority, expertise, confidence, voting power. Expected: SemanticAmbiguity. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: collapsing authority/expertise/confidence/voting-power into a single AgentWeight=0.8 is SemanticAmbiguity; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.19 — Quorum ... ΣVotes≥q. For example q=2/3. This is a quorum rule.
rows.statement: Defines a quorum rule ΣVotes≥q (e.g. q=2/3).

rows.anchor: 87.20 — Experiment 9 ... Five authorized members, quorum=4, only three participate. Expected: DecisionNotValid. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: three participants against a quorum requirement of 4 (of 5 authorized members) makes the decision DecisionNotValid; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.21 — Quorum is a legitimacy constraint ... A quorum does not tell us which option is best. It tells us whether sufficient participation exists for the decision mechanism to operate legitimately.
rows.statement: Clarifies quorum is a legitimacy constraint (sufficient participation) not a substantive judgment about which option is best.

rows.anchor: 87.22 — Veto authority ... V_i(D)=1. Veto=True ⇒ DecisionRejected. Common for critical domains such as security or constitutional constraints.
rows.statement: Defines veto authority: V_i(D)=1 implies DecisionRejected, common for critical domains like security or constitutional constraints.

rows.anchor: 87.23 — Experiment 10 ... Nine members vote A. One authorized security veto rejects A. Expected: if the governance constitution grants that veto, A cannot be approved. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: a single authorized security veto overriding a 9-member majority vote for A means A cannot be approved, if the constitution grants that veto; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.24 — Veto is not preference aggregation ... A veto represents Constraint rather than ordinary preference. Constraint ≠ Preference.
rows.statement: Reinforces Constraint ≠ Preference: a veto is a constraint mechanism, not an ordinary preference input to aggregation.

rows.anchor: 87.25 — Collective decision function ... D*=F(Evidence,Preferences,Expertise,Authority,Constraints,Quorum,Veto,Policy). This is significantly more precise than D*=MajorityVote.
rows.statement: Defines the collective decision function D*=F(Evidence,Preferences,Expertise,Authority,Constraints,Quorum,Veto,Policy), far more precise than D*=MajorityVote.

type_signature.domain: Evidence x Preferences x Expertise x Authority x Constraints x Quorum x Veto x Policy

rows.anchor: 87.26 — Experiment 11 ... A proposal receives 70% support but violates a constitutional constraint. Expected: Rejected. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: a 70%-supported proposal that violates a constitutional constraint must be Rejected; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.27 — Majority cannot override constitutional constraints ... Constitution > Governance > CollectivePreference. Subject, of course, to the actual institutional constitution.
rows.statement: States the precedence Constitution > Governance > CollectivePreference (subject to the actual institutional constitution).

rows.anchor: 87.28 — Experiment 12 ... Board majority approves a prohibited action. Expected: Authorization=False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: a board majority approving a prohibited action results in Authorization=False; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.29 — Delegation ... An agent may delegate decision authority A→B. But delegation itself requires Authority_{A→B}.
rows.statement: Defines delegation A→B as itself requiring an Authority_{A→B} grant.

rows.anchor: 87.30 — Experiment 13 ... Agent A has authority. A delegates to B without being permitted to delegate. Expected: DelegationInvalid. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: an agent delegating authority without being permitted to delegate produces DelegationInvalid; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.31 — Delegation chains ... A→B→C. Auth(C)=Auth(A) ∩ Delegation_{A→B} ∩ Delegation_{B→C}.
rows.statement: Formalizes delegation chains A→B→C: Auth(C)=Auth(A) ∩ Delegation_{A→B} ∩ Delegation_{B→C}, valid only if each link is valid.

rows.anchor: 87.32 — Experiment 14 ... A delegates to B. B delegates to C. B lacks delegation rights. Expected: C does not acquire valid authority. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: a broken delegation chain (B lacking delegation rights) means C does not acquire valid authority; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.33 — Temporary delegation ... Auth(B,t) for t∈[t1,t2]. This connects Step 83 directly to collective choice.
rows.statement: Extends delegation with a temporal validity window Auth(B,t) for t∈[t1,t2], explicitly linking Step 83's temporal authority to collective choice.

lineage_claims.quote: This connects Step 83 directly to collective choice.

rows.anchor: 87.34 — Experiment 15 ... B is delegated authority until 17:00. B approves at 17:05. Expected: InvalidAuthorization. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: an approval at 17:05 after delegated authority expired at 17:00 is InvalidAuthorization; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.35 — Human and AI participants ... Should their preferences have equal voting power? There is no universal mathematical answer. It is an institutional design decision.
rows.statement: States that whether human and AI participants' preferences carry equal voting power has no universal mathematical answer — it is an institutional design decision.

rows.anchor: 87.36 — Experiment 16 ... AI provides strong technical evidence. AI has Authority=0. Human board has Authority>0. Expected: AI evidence may influence the decision but does not automatically constitute organizational authorization. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: strong AI-provided evidence may influence a decision but, with AI Authority=0, does not automatically constitute organizational authorization; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.37 — This is an important KnowledgeOS principle ... EvidenceContribution ≠ DecisionAuthority. An AI can be epistemically useful without being institutionally sovereign.
rows.statement: States EvidenceContribution ≠ DecisionAuthority: an AI can be epistemically useful without being institutionally sovereign.

rows.anchor: 87.38 — AI recommendation ... Recommendation_AI from Decision_Human. Recommendation ≠ Authorization.
rows.statement: Distinguishes Recommendation_AI from Decision_Human, restating Recommendation ≠ Authorization.

rows.anchor: 87.39 — Experiment 17 ... AI recommends Approve. Human authorized decision-maker selects Reject. Expected: organization's decision is Reject, assuming the human is the authorized decision-maker. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: when AI recommends Approve but the human authorized decision-maker selects Reject, the organization's decision is Reject; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.40 — AI as one epistemic participant ... AI can instead contribute Evidence, Analysis, Prediction, Counterfactual, Recommendation. The governance layer decides what institutional authority those outputs carry.
rows.statement: Reframes AI as an epistemic participant contributing Evidence/Analysis/Prediction/Counterfactual/Recommendation, with the governance layer deciding what institutional authority those outputs carry.

rows.anchor: 87.41 — Strategic voting ... True preference A≻B but reporting B≻A improves the agent's outcome. Then truthful voting is not incentive compatible.
rows.statement: Illustrates strategic voting: an agent misreporting a preference (reporting B≻A while truly preferring A≻B) to improve its outcome, showing truthful voting is not always incentive compatible.

rows.anchor: 87.42 — Experiment 18 ... Agent strategically votes for B despite preferring A. Expected: StrategicVoting. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: an agent voting for B despite preferring A is StrategicVoting; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.43 — Agenda manipulation ... controlling the order in which alternatives are considered. A different ordering can produce a different final winner.
rows.statement: Describes agenda manipulation: the order in which alternatives are paired/considered (e.g. A vs B first, then winner vs C) can change the final collective-choice winner.

rows.anchor: 87.44 — Experiment 19 ... Same preferences. Agenda 1 produces A. Agenda 2 produces C. Expected: AgendaSensitivity. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: the same underlying preferences producing different winners (A vs C) under different agendas demonstrates AgendaSensitivity; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.45 — Governance implication ... The person controlling the agenda may possess substantial effective power even without formal voting authority. FormalAuthority ≠ EffectiveInfluence.
rows.statement: States FormalAuthority ≠ EffectiveInfluence: the agenda-controller may hold substantial effective power without formal voting rights.

rows.anchor: 87.46 — Experiment 20 ... Chair cannot vote but controls agenda, information presented, sequencing. Expected: Chair may still materially influence the outcome. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: a non-voting chair controlling agenda/information/sequencing may still materially influence the outcome; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.47 — Information framing ... If the decision-maker sees EvidenceSet_1 instead of EvidenceSet_2, the decision may change. InformationSelection is itself a governance concern.
rows.statement: Argues information framing/selection (which evidence set a decision-maker sees) can change the decision outcome, making InformationSelection itself a governance concern.

rows.anchor: 87.48 — Experiment 21 ... Decision committee sees only favorable evidence. Expected: SelectionBias. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: a committee shown only favorable evidence exhibits SelectionBias; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.49 — KnowledgeOS can improve this ... because KnowledgeOS has provenance and evidence lineage, it can potentially present SupportingEvidence and ContradictingEvidence together.
rows.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS's provenance/evidence lineage lets it present both supporting and contradicting evidence together, mitigating selection bias.

rows.anchor: 87.50 — Experiment 22 ... Claim C=True. KnowledgeOS finds E_1→C and E_2→¬C. Expected: Decision-maker sees the conflict rather than only the supporting evidence. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: a claim C=True with both supporting (E_1) and contradicting (E_2) evidence must be shown to the decision-maker as a conflict, not just the supporting side; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.51 — Epistemic disagreement ... agents disagree about P(H). We should not necessarily aggregate their probabilities by majority vote. Instead we may need P_i(H) and evidence quality Q_i.
rows.statement: Argues probability disagreements P_i(H) among agents should not be resolved by majority vote alone; evidence quality Q_i per agent may be needed.

rows.anchor: 87.52 — Experiment 23 ... Agent A: P(H)=0.9 based on strong evidence. Agent B: P(H)=0.1 based on weak evidence. Simple average: 0.5. Expected: UnsupportedProbabilityAggregation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: naively averaging P(H)=0.9 (strong evidence) and P(H)=0.1 (weak evidence) to 0.5 is UnsupportedProbabilityAggregation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.53 — Evidence-weighted aggregation ... A more principled approach may use a formal evidence-combination model. But again Weight must have semantics. We cannot simply invent Q_A=0.9.
rows.statement: Notes that a more principled evidence-weighted aggregation still requires the weight Q_A to have genuine semantics, not be invented arbitrarily (e.g. Q_A=0.9).

rows.anchor: 87.54 — Experiment 24 ... Evidence quality score 0.8 is used as though it were P(E|H). Expected: SemanticError. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: treating an evidence-quality score (0.8) as though it were the likelihood P(E|H) is SemanticError; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.55 — Consensus ... Consensus is different from majority. forall i: Accept(D) after discussion. But consensus can be expensive and may permit strategic obstruction.
rows.statement: Defines consensus (∀i: Accept(D) after discussion) as distinct from majority, noting it can be expensive and vulnerable to strategic obstruction.

rows.anchor: 87.56 — Experiment 25 ... One member refuses every proposal. Consensus becomes impossible. Expected: ConsensusFailure. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: a single perpetually-refusing member makes consensus impossible — ConsensusFailure; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.57 — Supermajority ... Threshold>1/2, e.g. 2/3. This makes reversal harder than ordinary majority.
rows.statement: Defines supermajority as a threshold above 1/2 (e.g. 2/3), making reversal harder than ordinary majority.

rows.anchor: 87.58 — Experiment 26 ... A constitutional change requires 2/3. A simple 51% majority cannot enact it. Expected: Rejected. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 26: a 51% majority cannot enact a change requiring 2/3 supermajority; expected Rejected; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.59 — Different decisions require different aggregation rules ... Routine decision: SimpleMajority. Architecture exception: Supermajority. Security-critical decision: SecurityVeto. Constitutional change: SpecialProcedure. AggregationRule=f(DecisionType).
rows.statement: States AggregationRule=f(DecisionType), mapping routine decisions to SimpleMajority, architecture exceptions to Supermajority, security-critical decisions to SecurityVeto, and constitutional changes to SpecialProcedure.

rows.anchor: 87.60 — Experiment 27 ... System uses simple majority for every decision type. Expected: GovernanceModelTooCoarse. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: using simple majority uniformly for every decision type is GovernanceModelTooCoarse; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.61 — Decision classification precedes aggregation ... DecisionType→AggregationRule. This is structurally similar to the architecture governance classification we developed earlier.
rows.statement: States DecisionType→AggregationRule as a structural analogue to earlier architecture-governance classification work.

rows.anchor: 87.62 — Collective decision state ... D=(Question,Evidence,Alternatives,Participants,Preferences,Authority,Constraints,AggregationRule,Result,Rationale). This makes the decision reconstructable.
rows.statement: Defines a full collective-decision record tuple D=(Question,Evidence,Alternatives,Participants,Preferences,Authority,Constraints,AggregationRule,Result,Rationale) for reconstructability.

type_signature.domain: Question x Evidence x Alternatives x Participants x Preferences x Authority x Constraints x AggregationRule

rows.anchor: 87.63 — Experiment 28 ... System stores only Result=A. Expected: it cannot reconstruct who participated, what evidence was used, which rule was applied, whether quorum existed. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: storing only Result=A loses the ability to reconstruct participants, evidence, applied rule, and quorum status; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.64 — Decision provenance ... Decision←Evidence, Decision←Authority, Decision←AggregationRule, Decision←Constraints. This fits perfectly into our existing provenance graph.
rows.statement: Restates decision provenance edges (Decision←Evidence/Authority/AggregationRule/Constraints) as consistent with the existing provenance graph.

rows.anchor: 87.65 — Historical collective decisions ... Combining Steps 83 and 87: Decision(t) depends on Evidence(t), Authority(t), Policy(t), AggregationRule(t). Historical decisions can be reconstructed.
rows.statement: Combines Step 83's temporal model with Step 87's aggregation model: Decision(t) depends on Evidence(t), Authority(t), Policy(t), AggregationRule(t), enabling historical reconstruction.

lineage_claims.quote: Combining Steps 83 and 87

rows.anchor: 87.66 — Experiment 29 ... Decision made in 2025. Aggregation rule changed in 2026. System replays the 2025 decision using the 2026 rule. Expected: HistoricalDecisionCorruption. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: replaying a 2025 decision using the 2026 (changed) aggregation rule is HistoricalDecisionCorruption; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.67 — Collective decision under uncertainty ... P(Y|D) with Authority(D). BestDecision does not necessarily mean HighestProbabilityOutcome. It means the authorized mechanism selected the action under the applicable decision model.
rows.statement: Argues BestDecision means the authorized mechanism selected the action under the applicable decision model, not necessarily the highest-probability outcome.

rows.anchor: 87.68 — Experiment 30 ... Option A: ExpectedUtility=90. Option B: ExpectedUtility=80. A violates a mandatory constraint. Expected: B. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: option A (ExpectedUtility=90) violating a mandatory constraint yields choice B (ExpectedUtility=80) instead; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.69 — The emerging hierarchy ... Truth ≠ Belief ≠ Preference ≠ Recommendation ≠ Decision ≠ Authorization. This may be one of the most important distinctions established in the entire mathematical sequence.
rows.statement: States the six-way distinction Truth ≠ Belief ≠ Preference ≠ Recommendation ≠ Decision ≠ Authorization, called possibly the most important distinction in the entire sequence.

rows.anchor: 87.70 — KnowledgeOS should preserve these categories ... Truth: what is the case? Belief: what does an agent believe? Evidence: why do we believe it? Preference: what outcome does an agent want? Recommendation: what does the model suggest? Decision: what has the authorized institution chosen? Author
rows.statement: Defines the semantics of each category in the hierarchy: Truth (what is the case), Belief (what an agent believes), Evidence (why we believe it), Preference (what an agent wants), Recommendation (what the model suggests), Decision (what the authorized institution chose), Authorization (what is permitted).

rows.anchor: 87.71 — Experiment 31 ... System stores all seven as status. Expected: SemanticCollapse. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 31: collapsing all seven categories (Truth/Belief/Evidence/Preference/Recommendation/Decision/Authorization) into a single 'status' field is SemanticCollapse; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.72 — This prevents a major AI failure mode ... AI may produce 'I recommend approving the change.' That is Recommendation. It must not silently become Decision. And even a valid decision does not automatically become Authorization.
rows.statement: Names a major AI failure mode prevented by the hierarchy: an AI recommendation silently becoming a Decision, or a valid Decision silently becoming Authorization.

rows.anchor: 87.73 — Experiment 32 ... AI output Recommendation=Approve. System executes production deployment automatically. Expected: UnauthorizedTransition unless the AI explicitly possesses the required authority under the governance model. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 32: a system auto-executing a production deployment from an AI Recommendation=Approve (without explicit AI authority under governance) is UnauthorizedTransition; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 87.74 — Collective choice and KnowledgeOS ... KnowledgeOS should not merely aggregate answers; it should preserve the institutional semantics of how a decision became legitimate.
rows.statement: States the architecture principle: KnowledgeOS should preserve the institutional semantics of how a decision became legitimate, not merely aggregate answers.

rows.anchor: 87.75 — New invariants: I_Aggregation, I_AuthorityExpertise, I_CollectiveConstraint, I_Quorum, I_Delegation, I_HistoricalAggregation, I_RecommendationDecision, I_DecisionAuthorization
rows.statement: States eight new invariants: I_Aggregation (every collective decision must use an explicitly defined aggregation mechanism), I_AuthorityExpertise (expertise, evidence quality, preference, and decision authority must not be conflated), I_CollectiveConstraint (collective preference cannot override higher-order mandatory constraints), I_Quorum (a decision requiring quorum must not become valid without sufficient authorized participation), I_Delegation (delegated authority cannot exceed the authority validly delegated by the delegator), I_HistoricalAggregation (historical decisions must be interpreted using the aggregation rules valid at decision time), I_RecommendationDecision (recommendation must not automatically become decision without required authority), I_DecisionAuthorization (a decision does not automatically grant execution authority unless the governance model explicitly defines that transition).

rows.anchor: 87.76 — Step 87 verdict: STEP 87 — PASS ... KnowledgeOS now has to distinguish at least six fundamentally different mathematical/institutional objects: Evidence→Belief→Preference→Recommendation→Decision→Authorization, while Truth exists independently of whether anyone currently knows or believes it.
rows.statement: Records Step 87 verdict PASS: KnowledgeOS must distinguish six objects (Evidence→Belief→Preference→Recommendation→Decision→Authorization) while Truth exists independently of anyone's knowledge/belief.

rows.anchor: The model is becoming remarkably coherent ... Truth→Observation→Evidence→Knowledge/Belief→Causal+Statistical Model→Prediction/Counterfactual→Recommendation→Collective Decision→Authorization→Action→Outcome→Observation. Across this loop Time+Uncertainty+Provenance+Causality+Incentives+Governance remai
rows.statement: Presents the cumulative full-loop pipeline after Step 87 (Truth→Observation→Evidence→Knowledge/Belief→Causal+Statistical Model→Prediction/Counterfactual→Recommendation→Collective Decision→Authorization→Action→Outcome→Observation), cross-cut by Time, Uncertainty, Provenance, Causality, Incentives, Governance.

rows.anchor: Step 88 — Next mathematical boundary: information theory ... How much information do we actually have, and how much information is required to make a reliable decision? Entropy, MutualInformation, InformationGain, SufficientStatistics, Compression, Lossy versus lossless knowledge, Minimum informatio
rows.statement: Previews Step 88: moves to information theory — entropy, mutual information, information gain, sufficient statistics, compression, lossy vs lossless knowledge, minimum information required for a decision — centered on whether compression/summarization/embedding/indexing of organizational knowledge can lose information that changes a decision.

rows.anchor: Step 87 — Next boundary: collective choice and aggregation ... When several legitimate agents disagree, how does the system produce one collective decision? F(Preferences_1,...,Preferences_n)→CollectiveDecision. voting theory; preference aggregation; consensus; quorum; veto; weighted authority; rank
rows.statement: Previews Step 87: collective choice/preference aggregation F(Preferences_1..Preferences_n)→CollectiveDecision, covering voting theory, consensus, quorum, veto, weighted authority, ranking aggregation, Arrow-type impossibility, strategic voting, agenda manipulation, minority rights, delegation, and the distinction between epistemic consensus and legitimate authority.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 87 — Next boundary: collective choice and aggregation

rows.anchor: 97.16 — Collective decisions ... D=f(V_1,...,V_n). Majority(V), Unanimity(V), WeightedVote(V).
rows.statement: Restates collective-decision aggregation D=f(V_1..V_n) via Majority, Unanimity, or WeightedVote rules.

rows.anchor: 97.17 — Experiment 8 ... Committee has 5 members. Votes: 3 Yes, 2 No. Rule: Majority. Expected: Decision=Yes. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8 confirms a simple majority vote (3-2) yields Decision=Yes under a Majority rule; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 97.18 — Majority does not mean truth ... Majority ≠ Truth. A majority produces a legitimate decision only because the governance constitution defines the rule.
rows.statement: Restates Majority ≠ Truth: a majority vote is legitimate only because the constitution defines that rule, not because it establishes truth.

rows.anchor: 97.19 — Experiment 9 ... Five experts vote 5 No. Evidence strongly establishes Risk=True. Expected: the unanimous vote does not make Risk=False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: a unanimous 5-No vote does not make Risk=False when evidence strongly establishes Risk=True; result PASS.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 87.49 — KnowledgeOS can improve this ... because KnowledgeOS has provenance and evidence lineage, it can potentially present SupportingEvidence and ContradictingEvidence together.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS's provenance/evidence lineage lets it present both supporting and contradicting evidence together, mitigating selection bias.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 87.51 — Epistemic disagreement ... agents disagree about P(H). We should not necessarily aggregate their probabilities by majority vote. Instead we may need P_i(H) and evidence quality Q_i.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues probability disagreements P_i(H) among agents should not be resolved by majority vote alone; evidence quality Q_i per agent may be needed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 87.53 — Evidence-weighted aggregation ... A more principled approach may use a formal evidence-combination model. But again Weight must have semantics. We cannot simply invent Q_A=0.9.
rationale_evidence.statement: Notes that a more principled evidence-weighted aggregation still requires the weight Q_A to have genuine semantics, not be invented arbitrarily (e.g. Q_A=0.9).

rationale_evidence.anchor: 87.67 — Collective decision under uncertainty ... P(Y|D) with Authority(D). BestDecision does not necessarily mean HighestProbabilityOutcome. It means the authorized mechanism selected the action under the applicable decision model.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues BestDecision means the authorized mechanism selected the action under the applicable decision model, not necessarily the highest-probability outcome.

aliases: Epistemic Resource Allocation, Attention Scheduling, Knowledge Triage and Portfolio Optimization

sources.note: S0929's Step 35: generalizes the single-decision Next-Best-Epistemic-Action into an organization-wide epistemic portfolio optimization across many competing uncertainties, introducing epistemic debt, bottleneck value, synergy/redundancy, Pareto frontiers, human-expert scheduling, and a four-level (Claim/Investigation/Decision/Portfolio) optimization hierarchy, plus an explicit anti-Goodhart's-Law objective correction.

rows.anchor: An enterprise does not have only one uncertainty ... U_1,...,U_n ... resources are finite ... How should KnowledgeOS allocate limited epistemic resources across competing uncertainties and decisions?
rows.statement: Generalizes NextBestEpistemicAction (single decision) to organization-wide resource allocation across many competing uncertainties.

lineage_claims.quote: We now continue from Step 34.

rows.anchor: mathcal U={u_1,...,u_n} unresolved knowledge problems ... mathcal R={r_1,...,r_m} available resources ... Allocate(mathcal R,mathcal U) to maximize decision quality
rows.statement: Formally defines the central resource-allocation problem Allocate(R,U).

rows.anchor: A conventional backlog might assign Priority=High/Medium/Low. That is insufficient ... Cost(U_1)=1 and Cost(U_2)=100. Their resource efficiency differs dramatically
rows.statement: Rejects simple High/Medium/Low prioritization as insufficient once cost varies dramatically.

rows.anchor: EU(u) as the expected improvement in decision quality resulting from resolving uncertainty u ... Efficiency(u)=EU(u)/Cost(u). But we need more dimensions
rows.statement: Defines epistemic utility and a first cost-efficiency ratio, noting it is insufficient alone.

rows.anchor: Priority(u)=f(Risk,DecisionImpact,VOI,Urgency,Dependency,Freshness,Cost). We should resist collapsing these prematurely into one scalar
rows.statement: Formalizes a multi-dimensional priority function and warns against premature scalar collapse.

rows.anchor: Priority=0.83. What does that mean? It hides why the item matters ... Score != Explanation. KnowledgeOS should preserve the underlying vector
rows.statement: States a single priority score hides explanatory information, giving the principle Score != Explanation.

rows.anchor: P(u)=(Impact,Risk,VOI,Urgency,Dependency,Freshness,Cost,Authority) ... Only at the optimization boundary may we derive a ranking
rows.statement: Defines the epistemic priority vector as the preserved, informative representation, deferring scalar ranking to the optimization boundary.

rows.anchor: C(d) in {Low,Medium,High,Critical}. This is domain/governance information. KnowledgeOS should not decide what Critical means
rows.statement: Defines decision criticality as domain/governance-owned information, not KnowledgeOS-decided.

rows.anchor: Impact(u,d) ... unknown backup restorability may have Impact(u_1,d_migration)=High
rows.statement: Defines uncertainty impact on a specific decision, worked with a backup-restorability example.

rows.anchor: u_1 -> A -> M -> D_1,D_2,D_3 ... u_1 influences several decisions. This gives Centrality(u_1) high value
rows.statement: Defines dependency centrality of an uncertainty influencing multiple decisions.

rows.anchor: Degree(u), Betweenness(u), Reachability(u) ... graph-theoretic indicators. But they are not automatically epistemic importance. A highly connected irrelevant node can still be irrelevant
rows.statement: Warns that raw graph-theoretic centrality measures are not automatically epistemic importance.

rows.anchor: DWC(u) = sum_d Criticality(d)*Impact(u,d). This is a conceptual formulation
rows.statement: Formalizes decision-weighted centrality combining decision criticality and per-decision impact.

rows.anchor: Urgency(u,t) ... Deadline(d)-t may approach zero. Then the value of resolving u can increase sharply
rows.statement: Defines urgency as a time-dependent factor that can sharply increase resolution value near a deadline.

rows.anchor: Freshness(u,t) ... InfrastructureState decays quickly ... ArchitecturalPrinciple decays slowly. freshness is domain-specific
rows.statement: Defines knowledge freshness as domain-specific, contrasting fast-decaying infrastructure state with slow-decaying architectural principles.

rows.anchor: HL(u) as the characteristic time over which knowledge becomes stale ... useful for scheduling revalidation
rows.statement: Defines a conceptual knowledge half-life for scheduling revalidation.

rows.anchor: EpistemicDebt is accumulated unresolved uncertainty that can impair future decisions ... undocumented infrastructure; stale architecture decisions; unverified assumptions; unresolved conflicting requirements; missing provenance
rows.statement: Introduces Epistemic Debt as accumulated unresolved uncertainty impairing future decisions, with five worked examples.

rows.anchor: Technical debt: ShortTermSpeed->FutureCost. Epistemic debt: UnresolvedUncertainty->FutureDecisionRisk. EpistemicDebt=DeferredKnowledgeWork with future decision consequences
rows.statement: Analogizes epistemic debt to technical debt and formalizes it as deferred knowledge work with future decision consequences.

rows.anchor: D_E(t+1)=D_E(t)+NewUncertainty-ResolvedUncertainty+Staleness. This is conceptual rather than a universal accounting equation
rows.statement: Proposes a conceptual debt-accumulation recurrence, explicitly not a universal accounting equation.

rows.anchor: U_1 remains unresolved. It becomes an assumption in M_1 ... an assumption in D_1. The original uncertainty now propagates. Unresolved uncertainty can compound
rows.statement: States unresolved uncertainty can compound as it becomes embedded as an assumption in downstream models and decisions.

rows.anchor: Blocker(u) ... u -> D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4, then resolving u may unlock substantial work. This is an epistemic bottleneck
rows.statement: Defines an epistemic bottleneck as an uncertainty blocking many downstream activities.

rows.anchor: BValue(u) = sum_d UnlockValue(d,u). This can be more important than uncertainty magnitude itself
rows.statement: Formalizes bottleneck value and states it can matter more than raw uncertainty magnitude.

rows.anchor: cannot determine whether a migration target supports a required database version ... architecture cannot finalize; infrastructure cannot provision; testing cannot complete; governance cannot approve. very high bottleneck value
rows.statement: Worked example of a high-bottleneck-value uncertainty blocking four downstream activity classes.

rows.anchor: Budget<=B, HumanHours<=H, Compute<=C, Time<=T. We now have a constrained optimization problem
rows.statement: Introduces multi-resource constraints forming a constrained optimization problem.

rows.anchor: x_i in {0,1} indicate whether investigation I_i is selected ... max sum_i x_i Value(I_i) subject to sum_i x_i Cost_i <= B. This resembles a knapsack problem
rows.statement: Formalizes basic epistemic portfolio selection as a 0/1-knapsack-like optimization.

rows.anchor: With many investigations and interactions, portfolio selection can become NP-hard in general ... Can KnowledgeOS run on a normal PC? Yes. But optimal portfolio allocation may require approximation or heuristics at large scale
rows.statement: States portfolio selection can be NP-hard in general, requiring approximation/heuristics at scale, while remaining feasible on ordinary hardware for smaller cases.

rows.anchor: For small numbers ExactOptimization may be practical. For large numbers Heuristic or GreedyApproximation may be preferable
rows.statement: Distinguishes exact from heuristic/greedy optimization by problem scale.

rows.anchor: I* = argmax_i NVOI(I_i)/Cost(I_i). Then repeat until the budget is exhausted. This is not globally optimal in every case, but often useful
rows.statement: Formalizes a greedy epistemic-allocation heuristic and notes its non-global-optimality.

rows.anchor: I_1 has moderate value alone. But I_1+I_2 unlock a very high-value decision. Value(I_1+I_2) > Value(I_1)+Value(I_2). There is complementarity. Greedy selection may miss this
rows.statement: Worked counterexample showing greedy allocation can miss complementary (synergistic) investigation pairs.

rows.anchor: Synergy(I_1,I_2) = Value(I_1,I_2) - Value(I_1) - Value(I_2). If Synergy>0, the investigations reinforce each other
rows.statement: Defines information synergy between two investigations.

rows.anchor: Synergy<0 may represent redundant investigations. This is common when two actions query the same underlying source
rows.statement: Defines redundancy as negative synergy, common for same-source investigations.

rows.anchor: Provenance -> Dependency -> Redundancy/Synergy -> ResourceAllocation. Now they become inputs to portfolio optimization
rows.statement: States portfolio optimization needs dependency information, chaining provenance and dependency graphs into redundancy/synergy detection and resource allocation.

rows.anchor: Expert_A infrastructure, Expert_B governance. I_1 requires A. I_2 requires B. We therefore need SkillMatch(I,Expert)
rows.statement: Defines a skill-match requirement for human-expert scheduling.

rows.anchor: An investigation cannot be assigned merely because the expert is available. We need Qualified(Expert,I). This becomes part of the action's admissibility
rows.statement: Defines expertise as an admissibility constraint, not merely availability.

rows.anchor: A human review can produce Observation, Interpretation, Decision, or Validation. It should therefore be represented as a structured epistemic event, not simply human approved = true
rows.statement: States human review must be represented as a structured epistemic event rather than a boolean approval flag.

rows.anchor: A human conclusion should preserve Who, When, Context, EvidenceReviewed, DecisionBasis. This makes human reasoning auditable
rows.statement: Defines required human-judgment provenance fields for auditability.

rows.anchor: Two experts may produce A and not-A. KnowledgeOS should preserve ExpertConflict. It should not simply average the experts
rows.statement: Requires preserving expert disagreement rather than averaging conflicting expert judgments.

rows.anchor: Reliability(Expert,Context) ... dangerous if generalized too broadly. excellent in Infrastructure but poor in LegalInterpretation. Reliability = f(Expert,Domain,Task)
rows.statement: Formalizes expert reliability as domain/task-specific and warns against over-generalizing it.

rows.anchor: A global ExpertScore=0.87 would be misleading. Expertise is contextual; task-specific; time-dependent; potentially changing
rows.statement: Rejects reducing expertise to a single permanent score.

rows.anchor: M_1 requires 1s, M_2 requires 10h. If both have similar decision value, M_1 wins on resource efficiency
rows.statement: Worked example of compute-cost-driven allocation preference between two models of similar value.

rows.anchor: Cost(I) = (c_money,c_time,c_human,c_compute,c_risk). Cost is a vector, not necessarily a scalar
rows.statement: Formalizes multi-resource cost as a vector quantity.

rows.anchor: I_1 dominates I_2 if Value(I_1)>=Value(I_2) and Cost_j(I_1)<=Cost_j(I_2) for every resource dimension j, with at least one strict inequality. Then I_2 can be eliminated
rows.statement: Defines Pareto dominance between investigations over vector costs.

rows.anchor: EpistemicParetoFrontier. This is useful before performing more expensive optimization
rows.statement: Defines the epistemic Pareto frontier as a pre-filter before expensive optimization.

rows.anchor: max_{S subseteq mathcal I} Value(S) subject to Resource(S)<=R ... Value(S) must account for interaction; redundancy; decision impact; risk reduction
rows.statement: Formalizes the general portfolio objective accounting for interaction, redundancy, decision impact and risk reduction.

rows.anchor: S_t is not fixed. After investigation I_t we obtain K_{t+1}. Then S_{t+1}=Optimize(K_{t+1}). This becomes a dynamic control problem
rows.statement: Extends the static portfolio to a dynamic re-optimization problem after each new observation.

rows.anchor: A practical architecture can optimize a short horizon t...t+h. Then re-evaluate after new information arrives. This avoids trying to predict the entire future
rows.statement: Proposes a receding-horizon strategy as a practical alternative to full-future prediction.

rows.anchor: Current Knowledge -> Identify Uncertainty -> Identify Decisions -> Calculate Impact -> Generate Investigations -> Estimate VOI/Cost/Risk -> Build Candidate Portfolio -> Apply Resource Constraints -> Select Next Action(s) -> Execute/Authorize -> Acquire Evidence -> Update Knowledge -> Recalculate ...
