aliases: GoF implementation extraction and architectural analysis

sources.note: The third and most implementation-detailed GoF-related artifact in the 2026-09-07 research day: a full 23-pattern implementation extraction with per-pattern KnowledgeOS candidate applications, an 11-mechanism reduction vocabulary, a proposed Design Pattern Registry schema, and a proposed follow-on KNOWLEDGEOS-DESIGN-PATTERN-CATALOG-2026-09 traceability matrix. Distinct from gof-design-patterns-as-falsification-lens-2026-09 (crosswalk/falsification of 6 candidates) and gof-variation-analysis-architectural-lens (principle-level variation-analysis method, KR-DESIGN-PATTERN-LENS-2026-09) from the same day.

rows.anchor: The book is not a collection of 23 classes to copy. It is a catalog of reusable implementation structures for isolating variation. ... Program to an interface, not an implementation ... Favor object composition over class inheritance ... Interface + Composition + Delegation + Polymorphism + Encapsulation
rows.statement: States the document's framing thesis: GoF is an implementation-mechanism catalogue, not a class library to copy, built from two core principles (program to an interface not an implementation; favor composition over inheritance) whose combined vocabulary is Interface + Composition + Delegation + Polymorphism + Encapsulation, of which the 23 patterns are specialized arrangements.

rows.anchor: Pattern = <Name, Intent, Motivation, Applicability, Structure, Participants, Collaborations, Consequences, Implementation, SampleCode, KnownUses, RelatedPatterns> ... A KnowledgeOS pattern record should therefore not merely store Pattern=Observer but ... identity/intent/problem/context/applicability/participants/collaborations/variation_point/implementation_mechanism/consequences/tradeoffs/known_uses/related_patterns/evidence/provenance
rows.statement: Extracts the GoF pattern-record template (12 fields) and proposes an analogous, richer KnowledgeOS Pattern record schema (15 fields including variation_point, evidence, and provenance) rather than storing only a pattern name.

rows.anchor: 4.1.1 Abstract Factory ... The factory owns the knowledge of concrete products ... KnowledgeFactory / PropositionFactory / EvidenceFactory / WarrantFactory / KnowledgeStateFactory ... should not be introduced automatically. It is justified only if KnowledgeOS must support multiple coherent families of epistemic implementations.
rows.statement: Abstract Factory (creational; isolates product-family creation behind AbstractFactory/AbstractProduct) proposed as a candidate KnowledgeFactory coordinating Proposition/Evidence/Warrant/KnowledgeState factories, explicitly gated on an actual need for multiple coherent families of epistemic implementations.

rows.anchor: 4.1.2 Builder ... The Builder allows the construction process to remain stable while different builders create different representations ... InquiryBuilder .domain(...).answerSpace(...).context(...).temporalScope(...).preservationContract(...).admissibility(...).build() ... strong candidate because KnowledgeOS objects contain explicit epistemic contracts.
rows.statement: Builder (stepwise construction separated from representation) proposed for complex epistemic objects (KnowledgeStateBuilder, EvidenceAssessmentBuilder, InquiryBuilder, DeterminationBuilder, DecisionBuilder), worked with a fluent InquiryBuilder example, rated a strong candidate given KnowledgeOS's explicit epistemic contracts.

rows.anchor: 4.1.3 Factory Method ... Factory Methods are commonly used inside Template Methods ... EvidenceAcquirer.acquire() / FileEvidenceAcquirer / DatabaseEvidenceAcquirer / ApiEvidenceAcquirer / HumanTestimonyAcquirer ... The higher-level process does not need to know which acquisition implementation is used.
rows.statement: Factory Method (subclasses determine concrete product at a point the framework knows must occur) proposed for pluggable EvidenceAcquirer implementations (File/Database/Api/HumanTestimony) so the higher-level acquisition process is implementation-agnostic; notes GoF's own observation that Factory Methods are commonly nested inside Template Methods.

rows.anchor: 4.1.4 Prototype ... shallow copy != deep copy ... PrototypeRegistry register/clone/unregister ... connects naturally with the KnowledgeOS Registry concept.
rows.statement: Prototype (creation by cloning configured examples, via a Prototype Manager/registry) proposed for Inquiry/Evidence-assessment/Knowledge-state/Research-workflow/Pattern templates through a PrototypeRegistry, with an explicit warning that shallow copy != deep copy matters for nested/circular structures.

rows.anchor: 4.1.5 Singleton ... Do not interpret Singleton as 'Every important service should be a Singleton.' ... Modern dependency injection often provides a better implementation mechanism. ... KnowledgeRegistry / PatternRegistry / SchemaRegistry might have singleton-like lifecycle semantics, but that does not mean the domain objects themselves should be Singleton objects.
rows.statement: Singleton (controlled single-instance access, book also discusses registry-based selection by name) is explicitly warned against as a general service-design rule for KnowledgeOS; only registries (Knowledge/Pattern/Schema) may have singleton-like lifecycle semantics, never domain objects themselves.

rows.anchor: 4.2.1 Adapter ... Object Adapter contains Adaptee; Class Adapter inherits Target and Adaptee ... LegacyEvidenceSource / ExternalEvidenceSource / LLMProvider / VectorStore / DocumentRepository / ExternalKnowledgeSystem ... lets KnowledgeOS preserve its own epistemic interface while adapting external systems.
rows.statement: Adapter (object-adapter vs class-adapter forms for reconciling incompatible interfaces) proposed for wrapping legacy/external evidence sources, LLM providers, vector stores, document repositories, and external knowledge systems behind a stable EvidenceSource interface.

rows.anchor: 4.2.2 Bridge ... The book explicitly separates the abstraction hierarchy from the implementation hierarchy ... KnowledgeRepresentation / RepresentationStore -> PostgreSQLStore/GraphStore/DocumentStore/EventStore ... aligns strongly with KnowledgeState != Representation.
rows.statement: Bridge (decoupling an abstraction hierarchy from an independently-varying implementation hierarchy, contrasted with the combinatorial-explosion Window/XWindow/PMWindow alternative) rated potentially one of the most important patterns, proposed for decoupling KnowledgeRepresentation from RepresentationStore backends (PostgreSQL/Graph/Document/Event), said to align strongly with the existing KnowledgeState != Representation distinction.

rows.anchor: 4.2.3 Composite ... individual objects and compositions of objects should be treated uniformly ... KnowledgeState -> Proposition/Evidence/Warrant/Determination/KnowledgeState ... EvidenceBundle -> Evidence, Evidence, EvidenceBundle ... supports hierarchical knowledge structures.
rows.statement: Composite (recursive Component/Leaf/Composite structure, with child management/parent references/transparency-vs-type-safety trade-offs) rated a very strong candidate for hierarchical KnowledgeState and EvidenceBundle structures.

rows.anchor: 4.2.4 Decorator ... Decorator identity is not the same as component identity. The book explicitly warns about this. That matters enormously for KnowledgeOS because identity and provenance are first-class concepts. ... Evidence -> ProvenancedEvidence -> AuditedEvidence -> SignedEvidence -> AccessControlledEvidence
rows.statement: Decorator (dynamically adding responsibilities via wrapping rather than subclass explosion) proposed for cross-cutting evidence capabilities (Provenanced/Audited/Signed/AccessControlled), with GoF's own warning carried forward that decorator identity differs from component identity -- flagged as critically important given KnowledgeOS's first-class identity/provenance concepts.

rows.anchor: 4.2.5 Facade ... KnowledgeOSFacade could expose inquire()/retrieveEvidence()/evaluateEvidence()/derive()/determine()/revise()/retract()/explain()/trace() while internally coordinating Inquiry/Evidence/Reasoning/Provenance/Knowledge-state/Decision/Governance subsystems.
rows.statement: Facade (simple client-facing interface coordinating a complex subsystem, book also suggests configuring the facade with replaceable subsystem objects rather than subclassing) rated a very strong candidate for a KnowledgeOSFacade exposing a stable nine-method API over seven internal subsystems.

rows.anchor: 4.2.6 Flyweight ... Separate IntrinsicState from ExtrinsicState ... Schema identifiers / Ontology terms / Pattern definitions / Vocabulary tokens / Canonical type descriptors / Shared proposition structures ... must be applied carefully because shared objects cannot contain context-specific state.
rows.statement: Flyweight (sharing objects factored into intrinsic vs extrinsic state via a FlyweightFactory) proposed for schema identifiers, ontology terms, pattern definitions, vocabulary tokens, canonical type descriptors, and shared proposition structures, with a warning that shared objects cannot carry context-specific state.

rows.anchor: 4.2.7 Proxy ... remote proxy, virtual proxy, protection proxy, smart reference, copy-on-write proxy ... EvidenceRepositoryProxy / KnowledgeStateProxy / RemoteKnowledgeProxy / AuthorizationProxy / LazyEvidenceProxy ... enforce authorization, lazy loading, remote access, caching, audit, rate limiting without changing the domain interface.
rows.statement: Proxy (controlling access to a RealSubject via one of five identified forms: remote/virtual/protection/smart-reference/copy-on-write) rated extremely relevant for AuthorizedKnowledgeProxy-style access control, lazy loading, remote access, caching, audit, and rate limiting over KnowledgeOS repositories without altering the domain interface.

rows.anchor: 4.3.1 Chain of Responsibility ... The book itself warns that receipt is not guaranteed. Therefore KnowledgeOS must represent Handled/NotHandled/NoEligibleHandler/Unauthorized/InsufficientEvidence rather than silently treating an unanswered request as failure or falsehood.
rows.statement: Chain of Responsibility (sequential handler forwarding without a hard-coded receiver) proposed for InquiryHandler routing across Cached/Local/Federated/HumanReview handlers, with an explicit epistemic requirement to represent five distinct non-response outcomes (Handled/NotHandled/NoEligibleHandler/Unauthorized/InsufficientEvidence) rather than collapsing an unhandled request into failure or falsehood.

rows.anchor: 4.3.2 Command ... ASSERT/LINK/REVISE/RETRACT/ISOLATE/DETERMINE/AUTHORIZE as Commands ... Command + PreState + PostState + Evidence + Actor + Timestamp + Authorization becomes an executable epistemic history. ... perhaps one of the strongest matches ... aligns very closely with KnowledgeOS's history-preserving state model.
rows.statement: Command (encapsulating a request as an object enabling queueing/logging/undo/redo/macro-commands) rated one of the strongest GoF matches: proposes representing epistemic operations (ASSERT/LINK/REVISE/RETRACT/ISOLATE/DETERMINE/AUTHORIZE) as Commands carrying Operation+PreState+PostState+Evidence+Actor+Timestamp+Authorization, forming an executable, auditable epistemic history.

rows.anchor: 4.3.3 Interpreter ... Interpreter does not solve parsing. ... Inquiry DSL / Knowledge query language / Evidence predicates / Policy expressions / Epistemic contracts / Governance rules ... complex languages should use parser/compiler technology rather than forcing every grammar into Interpreter.
rows.statement: Interpreter (recursive self-interpreting Expression tree / AST, explicitly connected to Composite, and explicitly not a parsing solution) proposed for an Inquiry DSL, knowledge query language, evidence predicates, policy expressions, epistemic contracts, and governance rules, with the book's own limitation carried forward -- complex grammars need real parser/compiler technology.

rows.anchor: 4.3.4 Iterator ... The book explicitly moves traversal responsibility out of the aggregate and into an iterator object. ... EvidenceGraph/KnowledgeGraph/KnowledgeState/ProvenanceGraph/InquiryGraph/CompositeEvidence ... allows traversal algorithms to remain independent of storage representation.
rows.statement: Iterator (First/Next/Current/IsDone traversal separated from the aggregate, with external/internal/recursive/cursor/null/privileged-access variants) rated essential for KnowledgeOS graphs (Evidence/Knowledge/Provenance/Inquiry) so traversal algorithms remain independent of storage representation.

rows.anchor: 4.3.5 Mediator ... Do not create a God Object called KnowledgeOSMediator. The book itself warns that the mediator can become a monolith. ... EpistemicCoordinator coordinating Inquiry/Evidence/Warrant/Reasoning/Determination/KnowledgeState/Governance.
rows.statement: Mediator (replacing many-to-many colleague coupling with central coordination; book notes Observer can implement Mediator notification) proposed as an EpistemicCoordinator, with an explicit repeated warning (consistent with S2864) against a monolithic 'KnowledgeOSMediator' God Object.

rows.anchor: 4.3.6 Memento ... KnowledgeStateSnapshot containing State/Version/Lineage/Contract/Timestamp ... KnowledgeOS can go further than classic Memento by preserving the complete transition history. Therefore Memento != Event History.
rows.statement: Memento (Originator/Memento/Caretaker with narrow/wide interfaces protecting internal state) proposed as a KnowledgeStateSnapshot (State/Version/Lineage/Contract/Timestamp) supporting restore/rollback/replay/audit/historical reconstruction, with the explicit distinction Memento != Event History since KnowledgeOS needs the complete transition history, not just point snapshots.

rows.anchor: 4.3.7 Observer ... push model, pull model, event-specific notification, ChangeManager, DAG-based update management ... An Observer notification is not evidence. This is a crucial KnowledgeOS distinction.
rows.statement: Observer (Subject/Observer state-change propagation, with push/pull/event-specific/ChangeManager/DAG-based variants) proposed for propagating KnowledgeState changes to EvidenceIndex/ExplanationCache/SearchIndex/GovernanceMonitor/DerivedKnowledge, with the crucial distinction that an Observer notification is not itself evidence.

rows.anchor: 4.3.8 State ... KnowledgeOS epistemic statuses are semantic concepts, not automatically GoF State objects. The pattern may implement them, but does not define their semantics. ... Candidate/Supported/Conflicted/Determined/Retracted/Superseded
rows.statement: State (delegating state-dependent behavior to state objects instead of conditionals, with five implementation-alternative variants) proposed for epistemic statuses (Candidate/Supported/Conflicted/Determined/Retracted/Superseded), with an explicit warning that the pattern can implement but never defines the semantics of these statuses.

rows.anchor: 4.3.9 Strategy ... The Context delegates the variable algorithm. ... ReasoningStrategy/EvidenceRankingStrategy/RetrievalStrategy/InferenceStrategy/ConflictResolutionStrategy/SimilarityStrategy/ReductionStrategy ... The epistemic engine remains stable while algorithms vary.
rows.statement: Strategy (interchangeable algorithm family behind a Context) rated a very strong candidate for seven named strategy families (Reasoning/EvidenceRanking/Retrieval/Inference/ConflictResolution/Similarity/Reduction), keeping the epistemic engine stable while computational algorithms vary.

rows.anchor: 4.3.10 Template Method ... collectEvidence()/validateEvidence()/constructWarrant()/reason()/evaluate()/determine()/record() with hooks validateSource()/evaluateReliability()/applyDomainRules() ... could encode the invariant epistemic pipeline without allowing arbitrary bypasses.
rows.statement: Template Method (invariant algorithm skeleton with variable steps/hooks) proposed as a KnowledgeEvaluationProcess with a fixed seven-step epistemic pipeline and three specialized hooks, framed as a way to prevent arbitrary bypasses of the invariant pipeline.

rows.anchor: 4.3.11 Visitor ... Visitor makes NewOperation cheap while making NewElementType expensive. ... ProvenanceVisitor/ExplanationVisitor/ValidationVisitor/DependencyVisitor/ImpactAnalysisVisitor/SerializationVisitor/AuditVisitor ... KnowledgeOS is likely to acquire new analyses more often than it acquires new fundamental epistemic object types.
rows.statement: Visitor (double-dispatch operations over a stable object structure, with the explicit new-operation-cheap/new-element-type-expensive trade-off) rated potentially one of the most powerful patterns for KnowledgeOS, given the prediction that new analyses (Provenance/Explanation/Validation/Dependency/ImpactAnalysis/Serialization/Audit) will be added more often than new fundamental epistemic object types -- exactly the situation GoF identifies as suitable for Visitor.

rows.anchor: The most important implementation matrix (23-row Pattern / What is isolated-varied / Primary mechanism table)
rows.statement: Consolidates all 23 patterns into a three-column table (Pattern, What is isolated/varied, Primary mechanism), e.g. Bridge=implementation/composition+abstraction, Command=request/request object, Visitor=operations over structure/double dispatch, stating the book itself provides essentially this 'what varies' view in its own design-variation table.

rows.anchor: I=Interface, C=Composition, D=Delegation, P=Polymorphism, H=Inheritance, R=Recursion, F=Factory/Creation, S=State, N=Notification, T=Traversal, V=Variation Encapsulation ... Strategy = Interface + Composition + Delegation ... Visitor = Interface + DoubleDispatch + Traversal ... This is more important than memorizing the 23 names.
rows.statement: Reduces the 23 GoF patterns to combinations of eleven primitive implementation mechanisms (Interface, Composition, Delegation, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Recursion, Factory/Creation, State, Notification, Traversal, Variation-Encapsulation), giving worked decompositions for Strategy, State, Decorator, Composite, Visitor, Command, Observer, and Bridge.

rows.anchor: real systems do not normally use one pattern in isolation ... Composite + Iterator + Visitor ... Command + Memento + Prototype (undo/redo) ... AbstractFactory + FactoryMethod + Singleton ... Architecture != Pattern. Instead: Architecture = Composition of appropriate patterns.
rows.statement: Argues (drawing on the book's own behavioral-pattern discussion) that patterns are normally combined, not used in isolation, giving three worked combinations, and concludes Architecture != Pattern but rather Architecture = Composition of appropriate patterns.

rows.anchor: The Lexi case study ... Composite -> document structure, Strategy -> formatting algorithms, Decorator -> UI embellishment, AbstractFactory -> look and feel, Bridge -> windowing platforms, Command -> undoable operations, Iterator -> traversal, Visitor -> analysis ... starts from design problems and constraints, then selects patterns.
rows.statement: Presents the book's Lexi document-editor case study (eight patterns applied to interacting design problems, not isolated textbook examples) as an architectural precedent KnowledgeOS should adopt: design problems and constraints first, pattern selection follows, exemplified by Lexi's choice of Visitor specifically because new analyses were expected more often than new element types.

rows.anchor: Translation into KnowledgeOS ... possible implementation architecture (Inquiry -> Evidence -> Warrant -> Reasoning -> Knowledge State -> Determine/Explain/Audit -> Decision/Analysis/Provenance) with a potential pattern allocation across Inquiry/Evidence/Warrant-Reasoning/Knowledge State/Storage-Infrastructure/Analysis ... This is an architectural hypothesis, not something derived from the GoF book itself.
rows.statement: Proposes a candidate whole-system implementation architecture pipeline plus a full pattern-to-subsystem allocation table, explicitly self-labeled as an architectural hypothesis rather than a conclusion GoF itself supports.

rows.anchor: 10.1 Command <-> state transition history ... C = <Operation, Actor, Arguments, PreState, Evidence, Authorization, PostState> ... 10.3 Composite <-> Knowledge State structure ... It does not provide the epistemic semantics. ... 10.4 Iterator <-> graph traversal: Graph != Iterator but Graph + Iterator -> Representation-independent traversal.
rows.statement: Details five 'particularly strong matches' with existing KnowledgeOS theory: Command as a seven-field executable/auditable transition record; Memento representing only a snapshot (not the full K0->K1->K2->K3 transition chain); Composite providing structure but not epistemic semantics; Iterator giving representation-independent traversal (Graph != Iterator, but Graph+Iterator -> representation-independent traversal); Strategy as a clean epistemic-algorithm-variation mapping.

rows.anchor: patterns should not be applied indiscriminately. They introduce indirection and can increase complexity and performance cost ... GoF pattern available not-implies GoF pattern required ... Pattern name not-implies Architecture decision ... Observed design problem -> Required variability -> Candidate pattern -> Alternative pattern(s) -> Trade-off analysis -> Implementation experiment -> Verification -> Architecture decision
rows.statement: Carries forward the book's own warning against indiscriminate pattern application (indirection/complexity/performance cost) into two governing non-implications (pattern-available !=> pattern-required; pattern-name !=> architecture-decision) and an eight-step required justification pipeline every KnowledgeOS pattern adoption must pass.

rows.anchor: GoF and the current KnowledgeOS minimality problem ... Observer is implemented using interface/registration/collection/notification/delegation ... Pattern != Primitive and Pattern != Capability and Pattern != KernelOperation ... A GoF pattern can help implement a capability, but it cannot by itself establish that the capability is necessary.
rows.statement: Connects the implementation-mechanism decomposition (e.g. Observer, Strategy each decomposing into more primitive mechanisms) to the open K_min (kernel minimality) research question, stating Pattern != Primitive, Pattern != Capability, and Pattern != KernelOperation, and that a pattern implementing a capability never by itself establishes that capability's necessity.

rows.anchor: GoF gives us an implementation vocabulary (19-row table: Creation->Factory/Builder/Prototype ... RequestRouting->ChainOfResponsibility) ... What GoF does NOT give KnowledgeOS: Evidence, Warrant, Truth, Knowledge, Determination, Inquiry, epistemic uncertainty, epistemic contracts, provenance semantics, contradiction semantics, knowledge-state semantics, governance semantics. ... KnowledgeOS Theory -> Domain Semantics while GoF -> Implementation Structures. The two layers must not be confused.
rows.statement: Provides a design-concern-to-pattern vocabulary table, then an explicit list of eleven domain-semantic concepts GoF does not and cannot provide, concluding the two-layer separation KnowledgeOS Theory -> Domain Semantics vs GoF -> Implementation Structures must never be confused.

rows.anchor: The correct architecture relationship ... KnowledgeOS Theory -> Domain Concepts -> Required Capabilities -> Required Behaviors -> Design Problems -> Candidate Design Patterns -> Concrete Architecture -> Implementation -> Verification -> Governance ... Not: GoF Pattern -> Architecture -> Theory. The second direction would be backwards.
rows.statement: Specifies the mandatory nine-stage dependency direction from KnowledgeOS Theory down to Governance, and explicitly forbids the reverse GoF-Pattern-first direction as architecturally backwards.

rows.anchor: A KnowledgeOS Design Pattern Registry ... DesignPattern record with PatternId/Name/Classification/Intent/Problem/Applicability/VariationPoint/Participants/Collaborations/ImplementationMechanism/Consequences/KnownUses/RelatedPatterns/CandidateUseCases/Evidence/Verification/GovernanceStatus ... example DP-STRATEGY record with Status: Candidate, Architecture: Not yet ratified.
rows.statement: Proposes a concrete KnowledgeOS Design Pattern Registry record schema (16 fields) and a fully worked DP-STRATEGY example record, explicitly marked Status: Candidate / Architecture: Not yet ratified.

rows.anchor: The most important extracted lesson ... Identify what changes -> encapsulate the change -> program against a stable interface -> compose implementations -> evaluate consequences ... Find the variation before choosing the pattern. ... Seven principles P1-P7: Interface isolation, Encapsulate variation, Prefer composition, Delegate responsibility, Make runtime structures explicit, Combine patterns, Never apply a pattern without a design problem.
rows.statement: States the book's single deepest lesson as a five-step method and compresses the whole document into seven named implementation principles P1 (Interface isolation) through P7 (never apply a pattern without a design problem), the last restating that a pattern is justified by the variability/problem it solves, not by catalogue membership.

rows.anchor: GoF should become an implementation pattern library for KnowledgeOS, not the foundation of KnowledgeOS theory. ... Theory -> Semantic Model -> Capability -> Design Problem -> Pattern -> Implementation and never Pattern -> Capability -> Theory. ... Proposed next implementation artifact: KNOWLEDGEOS-DESIGN-PATTERN-CATALOG-2026-09 ... 23 GoF Patterns x KnowledgeOS Capabilities, classified as Applicable/Candidate/Unnecessary/Contradictory/Unknown.
rows.statement: Final governance conclusion and next-artifact proposal: GoF is to become an implementation pattern library (never a theory foundation), with the mandated six-stage dependency chain restated, and a proposed next artifact KNOWLEDGEOS-DESIGN-PATTERN-CATALOG-2026-09 that would classify every 23-patterns x KnowledgeOS-capabilities intersection into one of five statuses; explicit bottom line: do not implement all 23 patterns, build a GoF -> KnowledgeOS capability traceability matrix instead so every adoption is justified by an actual design problem.
