rows.statement: Finds theory-extraction/02-ELEMENT-INDEX.md already carries the exact homonym criterion that G-22 spent a full investigation re-deriving: 'if X's definition contains Y, then X != Y' (e.g. K=(K,H) and K=(K,C,T,E,A) both contain K, so K is a structure that HAS K, not a spelling of it); applying this rule reportedly cut candidate K-definitions from 10 to 4 and reduced comparison pairs from 45 to 6.

rows.anchor: Reconciliation matrix ... G-01 ... EC was not lost, it MOVED to Γ; codomain half answered as mis-posed ... RE-SCOPE (both halves)
rows.statement: G-01 (why did Satisfied(K,r,EC) lose EC, and how did a 9/10-valued codomain become 3-valued?): finds theory-extraction/105-READ-RECORD shows the evaluator Gamma(E,Q,C,EC) still carries EC, so the premise that EC was lost is too strong -- it MOVED to Gamma, not disappeared; and the codomain question is separately judged mis-posed (U is overloaded three ways; the correct move is to discover the codomain rather than presuppose it). Action: RE-SCOPE both halves; flagged in the adversarial check as resting on an unverified assumption that Gamma's EC is the same EC as 025d's, recorded as [PROPOSED] not [EMP].

rows.statement: G-05 (is R_req(Q,Gamma) a descendant of R(P), or an independent reuse?): finds R_req={d_1..d_k} with a preservation condition has zero citations of R(P)/025d, though one line derives R_req from 'minimal operational tasks required' (purpose-like). rows.anchor: G-09 ... 025d refuses a scalar for Zero, on incomparability of requirement kinds; 025r gives ExpectedLoss = Σ_s P(s|E)L(a,s) ... hypothesis CONFIRMED at source ... The gap existed only because the two were compared as if one object.
rows.statement: G-09 (is the operative distinction loss-over-actions vs collapse-of-an-assessment?): verified at both endpoints that 025d refuses a scalar specifically for Zero on incomparability-of-requirement-kinds grounds ('one missing governance approval could be more blocking than five low-priority informational gaps'), while 025r's ExpectedLoss=sum_s P(s|E)L(a,s) sums over states given evidence, indexed by action -- a different index set entirely, and 025r itself warns risk should not be reduced to probability. Verdict: DISTINCT, no conflict at either historical timepoint. Action: CLOSE -- called 'the cleanest case of the discipline paying off': the gap existed only because two non-comparable objects were compared as if one.

rows.anchor: C-1 ... 025d forbids a scalar; the 09-02 Loss_{ℛ_req}(π) is a scalar sum ... the 09-02 lane has TWO renderings of one object ... the real question is may a priority weighting be stipulated? Not adjudicated; both branches preserved.
rows.statement: C-1 (does 025d's scalar-refusal contradict a 09-02 scalar Loss_req?): finds the 09-02 lane itself has TWO renderings of one object -- 20260902-182008's RREQ-6 renders Loss_req as a SET (Loss_req = R_req ∩ Collapsed(pi), adequacy = empty-set) while 20260902-182016 L217 renders it as a weighted SCALAR (sum w_i·I(Collapse), adequacy == 0 for P1), and the scalar rendering supplies priority weights -- exactly the comparability whose absence was 025d's stated reason for refusing a scalar. Verdict: the contradiction is internal to the 09-02 lane, not cross-lane with 025d; re-scoped to the real, un-adjudicated normative question 'may a priority weighting be stipulated?', with both renderings explicitly preserved rather than resolved. Notes the two 09-02 files' mtimes/filename-stamps disagree on ordering, recorded but not used to infer precedence.

rows.anchor: TheoryState(t) — what actually changed, and what did not ... No earlier TheoryState(t) is altered by any row below.
rows.statement: States and applies a four-way discipline for every reconciled gap: (1) historical state at time t, (2) later discovery of evidence, (3) later adjudication, (4) present reconstruction status -- kept strictly separate so no earlier TheoryState(t) is ever altered or back-propagated by a later finding; worked through for G-01, G-06, G-07, G-09, C-1, G-15, G-21 in a table.

rows.statement: Runs a mandatory adversarial check against every proposed closure/re-scope, asking what would refute it and whether that was searched: G-07, G-09, G-15 survive fully scoped; G-16's closure is explicitly restricted to locatability once the RA-v1.1 homonym is found; C-1's re-scope survives since the two renderings have different adequacy conditions and types (not a mere gloss), though their mtimes disagree on order (recorded, not used for precedence); G-01's re-scope is REFUSED by its own check -- it rests on an unverified assumption that Gamma(E,Q,C,EC)'s EC is the same EC as 025d's, and the corpus has twice already been shown (Omega, K) to reuse glyphs across re-foundings, so this is recorded as [PROPOSED] not [EMP] and made the first obligation of the re-scoped gap.

rows.anchor: 5. What remains genuinely load-bearing ... G-05 (b-half) ... the same shape as the Ω-1 × Ω-2 homonym, and undecided
rows.statement: Summarizes what remains genuinely load-bearing after reconciliation: G-12 (180 of 265 unread files, every crossing lineage claim provisional); G-11 re-scoped (64 files, >=3 senses, two forming a corpus-declared TRUE CONTRADICTION, live simultaneously after step 285); G-05 b-half (whether R_req descends from R(P) -- explicitly compared in shape to the undecided Omega-1xOmega-2 homonym); G-06 (equiv_sem half, the identity question the whole K line depends on); G-21 per-sense (three of five Omega senses still unlocated); C-1 (now precisely 'may a priority weighting be stipulated?', correctly left un-adjudicated as normative); G-04 (correctly deferred by method).

rows.statement: States the closing scope discipline: nothing in this reconciliation was canonicalized -- no definition selected, no lineage fixed, no Omega/K/EC/Sat interpretation chosen; C-1's two branches remain both preserved rather than resolved; G-04 stays deferred; every 'closure' asserted here is only the claim that a question was already answered elsewhere, never that a theory question is settled. Reiterates the standing firewall: brainstorming/three_model_convergence/ was not opened, read, grepped or cited.

rows.anchor: 1. ⛔ G-01 — the premise is not 'too strong'. It is REFUTED, and it asked about the wrong argument ... The argument that was dropped is G, not EC. EC survives in five of the six forms.
rows.statement: Retracts the prior G-01 re-scope: a systematic inventory of STEP-VERIFY-025a-025g.md finds six non-mutually-reduced forms of Zero inside 025d alone (a 5-tuple with EC_G; a shorthand set-difference form; a 4-tuple no longer a function of K/G/EC at all; a two-argument form Z_t=Zero(K_t,EC_t) where G is DROPPED; a form where K* replaces G and K* is never constructed; and a form using an operator symbol that collides with a different oplus meaning from 25C). Concludes the argument actually dropped across these forms is G, not EC -- EC survives in five of the six forms -- so the original G-01 premise is REFUTED, not merely too strong, and was asking about the wrong argument.

rows.anchor: The codomain never went 9/10 → 3. It went 9 → 10 → 11 and was never re-declared ... no document anywhere linking a 9/10-valued satisfaction codomain to a 3-valued one — the separately-recorded 3-value object is Σ = {Unknown, Supported, Refuted} ... a different object. My gap had silently joined them.
rows.statement: Finds the satisfaction-status codomain S grows 9 (25D.4) -> 10 (25D.7 adds Missing, itself used one section before being declared) -> 11 (25D.23 adds Failed) and is never re-declared afterward -- the final codomain of Status(K,r,EC) is nowhere fixed. Also finds no document anywhere links this 9/10/11-valued codomain to a separately-recorded 3-valued object Sigma={Unknown,Supported,Refuted} (DECISION-SIGMA-EPISTEMIC-STATUS.md) -- a different object entirely; the original G-01 gap had silently conflated the two.

rows.anchor: And Satisfied is a three-way homonym in one document ... three types under one name. The same defect as Ω-1 × Ω-2, inside one document, on one object, and already recorded in the verification lane.
rows.statement: Finds 'Satisfied' is used as three different types within one document (025d): an element of the status set S, a set-valued function Satisfied(K,R_G), and a predicate Satisfied(K,r,EC) -- explicitly identified as the same homonym defect pattern as the Omega-1 x Omega-2 collision, occurring inside one document on one object, and already recorded in the verification lane. Re-poses G-01 as three distinct questions: (i) why Zero carries six irreconcilable forms in 025d; (ii) why G is dropped at 25D.24 and replaced by K* at 25D.31; (iii) what fixes S after 11 values. The prior Gamma(E,Q,C,EC)-relocation framing is withdrawn as superseded, since EC was never lost.

rows.anchor: 2. ⭐ G-06 — upgrade RE-SCOPE → CLOSE. The ≡_sem half is answered too. ... KAID IS bounded-context-scoped SEMANTIC identity — that is the relation to ≡_sem. ... Context inside KAID is undefined ... closes into an existing open gap rather than remaining its own.
rows.statement: Upgrades G-06 from RE-SCOPE to CLOSE: STEP-VERIFY-025h-025z.md verbatim shows 025i SS37's provisional KAID=Identity(CanonicalAssertion,Context) is explicitly superseded by 025s SS43's 'Knowledge Atma is the stable semantic identity of an epistemic meaning within a bounded context' (with KAID != RecordID != EntityID), 025s SS36's three-level EntityIdentity/KnowledgeMeaningIdentity/RecordIdentity split, and 025i SS11's context-indexed equivalence family (x equiv_exact y, x equiv_struct y, x equiv_{sem,C} y). Concludes KAID IS bounded-context-scoped semantic identity, which is precisely its relation to equiv_sem -- but records an un-closed residue ('Context inside KAID is undefined, and its granularity determines everything') which is identical to the master register's own G-15 ('Context has no type, domain or equality anywhere'), so G-06 closes by folding into an already-open gap rather than remaining independently open.

rows.anchor: 3. ⚠️ G-07 — the closure stands; my stated reason was wrong ... TG-02 itself remains OPEN — so the closure is of my gap, not of the underlying sufficiency-signature question.
rows.statement: Confirms G-07's closure but corrects its stated reason: TG-02 actually concerns 'Sufficient has no signature' (relational sufficiency's parametricity defence is untested, e.g. a >=3-independent-sources rule with no formal independence relation), remains OPEN today with a verifier-recommended proposed signature and an TG-08 blocking dependency; the 'six-component vector' the earlier closure referenced is a DIFFERENT object (step-001 SS3's independence vector I(e_i,e_j)), itself separately recorded as LOST/UNACCOUNTED and never reused, with later treatments being independent re-derivations; TG-02 and 'six-component' never co-occur in any of the 464 verification files. Concludes G-07's literal misreading question is answered YES and the misreading is now correctly identified, but TG-02 itself (the underlying sufficiency-signature question) remains OPEN -- only the reconstruction's own gap is closed, not the theory question.

rows.statement: Reports the systematic inventory confirms several prior rows unchanged: G-09/C-1's ExpectedLoss and Loss_R_req objects appear in 0 of 464 verification files (NO RELEVANT MATCH, prior adjudication stands), corroborated by STEP-TRACE-B4 SS32 ('the four metric axioms are stated and Zero fails them', a Zero-scoped refusal); a THIRD C-1 endpoint is found in STEP-TRACE-B3 Q19 ('DISTANCE_REJECTED / DISCREPANCY_ADOPTED... scalar = policy decision instrument'), which answers the re-scoped normative question in one direction without fully adjudicating it; G-15 remains resolved (though the phrase 'Foundational Traceability Matrix' itself has 0 matches -- it is the reconstruction's own name, not a corpus artifact); G-16 is confirmed since no verification-tree file defines or constructs v1.1 at all (it exists only as a directory), strengthening a separate G-23; G-17 is confirmed FIREWALL-LIMITED (0 matches for checkpoint terms); G-05's RE-SCOPE stands with an added notation-provenance flag (R_req(Q,Gamma) as a form is written nowhere in the verification lane); G-08 stands unchanged (no document asserts or denies a common ancestor across the 025-series, 272a-277, and the 09-01/09-02 math lane).

sources.note: Step 279 (2026-08-30 23:04) is the commissioned executable-implementation step for Step 278's Policy-Authority governance model. Specifies 15 implementation components (Policy, Rule, Authority, Authorization evaluator, Conditional verdict, PolicyEvaluator algorithm, Rule-independence graph evaluator, Measurement evaluator, Calibration, PolicyVersioning, Temporal validity half-open interval, Overlap detector five-way classification, Historical replay, Policy change state machine, Governance event model, five bounded contexts / three aggregates: Policy, Authority, PolicyChange), an executable EvaluatePolicy pseudocode algorithm, and the same F1-F13 falsification programme from Step 278 now as executable test specs. Explicitly declares Step 279 != Empirical Closure and Step 279 != Governance Closure, and that PASS on a test != Theory Proven. An in-file supervisory review CONDITIONALLY ACCEPTS it, listing nine specific underspecification gaps (rule-combination logic, conditional-resolution-strategy execution, calibration procedure, F1-F13 execution specs, convergence conditions, aggregate commands/events, traceability test coverage, per-scale valid operations, deny-over-permit justification) and hands off to 'STEP 279 REVISED — EXECUTION' rather than directly to Step 280.

rows.anchor: Step 279 does not create new theory. It attempts to execute the existing theory and records exactly where formal specification survives contact with computation. ... $$\boxed{\text{Specification} \rightarrow \text{Implementation} \rightarrow \text{Execution} \rightarrow \text{Evidence}}$$ and not: $$\text{Specification} \rightarrow \text{Assumed correctness}.$$
rows.statement: States the governing methodological rule for Step 279: the pipeline must be Specification -> Implementation -> Execution -> Evidence, explicitly rejecting Specification -> Assumed correctness. The implementation prompt prohibits silently repairing failures or treating formal specification as empirical fact.

rows.anchor: Step 279 covers only the Policy and Authority governance layer. It MUST NOT redesign: K; Sigma; the transformation theory; the previously established epistemic model; bounded-context boundaries.
rows.statement: Explicitly scopes Step 279 to the Policy/Authority governance layer only, prohibiting redesign of K, Sigma, transformation theory, the epistemic model, or bounded-context boundaries -- treating those as fixed inputs.

rows.anchor: $$PID = Hash(content,rules,parameters,authority,validity)$$ ... A policy version is immutable after activation.
rows.statement: Implements Step 278's content-addressed policy identity: PID = Hash(content, rules, parameters, authority, validity), with a policy version treated as immutable after activation.

rows.anchor: The implementation MUST NOT: $$Unknown \rightarrow Deny$$ or: $$Conditional \rightarrow Permit.$$ These are explicitly prohibited fallback behaviours.
rows.statement: Prohibits two specific unsafe fallback behaviours in the authorization evaluator: an Unknown verdict must never be silently converted to Deny, and a Conditional verdict must never be silently converted to Permit.

rows.anchor: $$Scale \in \{Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio\}.$$ No arithmetic operation may be applied merely because a value is numerically encoded. In particular: $$Ordinal \not\Rightarrow Interval.$$
rows.statement: Mandates explicit measurement-scale typing (Nominal/Ordinal/Interval/Ratio) for any quantitative policy rule, forbidding arithmetic operations merely because a value is numerically encoded, and specifically forbidding treating an ordinal scale as if it were interval-scaled.
missing: enumeration of exactly which operations are valid per scale — flagged as a gap by the in-file supervisory review

rows.anchor: $$Calibration = (Model, ValidationData, CalibrationMetric)$$ and: $$CalibrationVerified \iff CalibrationMetric \le Threshold.$$ This prevents an asserted probability from being treated as automatically trustworthy merely because a model produced it.
rows.statement: Requires any probabilistic policy criterion (P(theta>c|X)>=q) to reference an explicit statistical model with a calibration triple (Model, ValidationData, CalibrationMetric) and threshold comparison, preventing an asserted probability from being automatically trusted merely because some model produced it.
missing: what Model/ValidationData/CalibrationMetric/Threshold concretely are — flagged HIGH severity by the in-file supervisory review

rows.anchor: | Dimension | Meaning | | Formal closure | Definitions and signatures are complete | | Computational closure | The specified operations execute | | Empirical closure | Behaviour is validated against real KnowledgeOS | | Governance closure | Required normative decisions are ratified | The implementation phase can establish at most the first two. Therefore: $$\boxed{Step\ 279 \neq Empirical\ Closure}$$ and: $$\boxed{Step\ 279 \neq Governance\ Closure}$$
rows.statement: Restates and applies the four-dimension closure taxonomy from Step 278 (Formal/Computational/Empirical/Governance), explicitly limiting what Step 279's implementation phase can establish to at most Formal and Computational closure; Empirical closure (validation against real KnowledgeOS) is reserved for Step 280, and Governance closure (ratified normative decisions) cannot be achieved through implementation at all. Explicitly forbids declaring 'KnowledgeOS Theory Complete' at this stage.

rows.anchor: A Governance aggregate MUST NOT directly mutate a KnowledgeState aggregate. Instead: Governance Command -> Governance Aggregate -> Governance Event -> Cross-context handler -> Knowledge/Transformation command -> Knowledge Aggregate. This preserves aggregate ownership and prevents governance from becoming a backdoor mutation mechanism.
rows.statement: Specifies a critical DDD invariant for the five-bounded-context implementation (Knowledge, Evidence, Assessment, Governance, History): a Governance aggregate must never directly mutate a KnowledgeState aggregate; changes must flow through a governance event and a cross-context handler that issues a proper Knowledge/Transformation command, preventing governance from becoming a backdoor mutation path.
invariants: Governance aggregate must not directly mutate a KnowledgeState aggregate

rows.anchor: $$\boxed{DENY \succ CONFLICT \succ CONDITIONAL \succ UNKNOWN \succ PASS}$$ ... Combine(results): if any DENY: return DENY ... The implementation MUST test whether: $$(a\oplus b)\oplus c = a\oplus(b\oplus c)$$ for the declared composition domain. If associativity does not hold, the reason MUST be documented.
rows.statement: Defines an explicit rule-combination algebra: a total precedence order DENY > CONFLICT > CONDITIONAL > UNKNOWN > PASS realized via a Combine() function, with an explicit requirement that the implementation test associativity of the combination operator over its declared domain, documenting the reason if associativity fails. This closes the gap the prior review labeled 'implicit rule-combination logic.'

rows.anchor: ### WAIT ... identify event/time trigger; persist pending evaluation; schedule reassessment ### REQUEST ... ### ESCALATE ... ### REASSESS ... ### BLOCK ... terminate requested operation; return governance denial; preserve reason and evidence
rows.statement: Operationalizes the five Conditional-verdict resolution strategies as executable procedures: WAIT (persist pending evaluation, schedule reassessment on trigger), REQUEST (create request to an actor/system, await response, attach resulting evidence), ESCALATE (create escalation to higher authority, preserve original evaluation), REASSESS (wait for changed evidence/context, re-run affected rules, preserve prior assessment), BLOCK (terminate the operation, return governance denial, preserve reason and evidence).

rows.anchor: $$Scope(o)\subseteq Scope(a)$$ and: $$Jurisdiction(o)\subseteq Jurisdiction(a).$$ If either condition fails: $$Authorize = Deny.$$ This is an executable invariant rather than a textual assumption.
rows.statement: Specifies an executable Authority Scope Invariant: any Permit result requires both Scope(operation) subseteq Scope(authority) and Jurisdiction(operation) subseteq Jurisdiction(authority); if either fails, the result must be Deny. Framed explicitly as an executable check rather than a mere textual assumption.
invariants: Scope(o) subseteq Scope(a) and Jurisdiction(o) subseteq Jurisdiction(a) whenever Authorize=Permit

rows.anchor: Calibrate(model, validation_data): generate predictions; compare predictions with observations; calculate declared calibration metric; compare metric against threshold; return: VERIFIED or FAILED ... Possible metrics include: Brier score; Expected Calibration Error; calibration slope/intercept. The implementation MUST record which metric was selected and why. A probability claim without a declared statistical model is: $$UNKNOWN.$$
rows.statement: Specifies a concrete calibration procedure (previously flagged HIGH severity as underspecified): Calibrate(model, validation_data) generates predictions, compares them with observations, computes a declared metric (Brier score, Expected Calibration Error, or calibration slope/intercept), compares against a threshold, and returns VERIFIED or FAILED; the metric choice must be recorded and justified, and any probability claim lacking a declared statistical model is classified UNKNOWN rather than trusted.

rows.anchor: $$L_i=Version(\pi_s)-Version(\pi_i).$$ Convergence occurs when: $$\forall i: L_i=0.$$ For an eventual-consistency implementation, define a finite convergence window \(\tau_c\). Then: $$\boxed{\forall i,\quad t\le t_0+\tau_c \Rightarrow Version(\pi_i)=Version(\pi_s)}$$ ... F12 passes only if convergence occurs within the declared bound. This converts "eventually reaches all nodes" into an actual executable criterion.
rows.statement: Defines a measurable governance-propagation convergence criterion: version lag L_i = Version(source) - Version(node_i), with convergence requiring a finite bound tau_c such that all nodes reach the source version by t0+tau_c; F12 now passes only if convergence is observed within this declared bound, replacing the previously vague 'eventually reaches all nodes' language with an executable criterion.

rows.statement: Provides fully specified, individually executable test protocols for all thirteen falsification tests F1-F13 (previously only named with an expected-yes result), each with an explicit SETUP, EXECUTE, OBSERVE, EXPECTED RESULT, PASS CONDITION, and FAIL CONDITION -- e.g. F1 (policy-free transition) requires T(K0,o) to yield exactly Unknown(NoApplicablePolicy), failing on Permit or unauthorized execution; F10 (historical replay) requires PolicyAt(t_old)=pi_1, failing if replay uses the current policy pi_2 instead.

rows.anchor: PRECEDENCE = [DENY, CONFLICT, CONDITIONAL, UNKNOWN, PASS] # 279 §7 ... def Combine(results: List[Verdict]) -> Verdict: if not results: return Verdict(INDETERMINATE,"NoResults") if any(v.value==DENY for v in results): return Verdict(DENY, ...) ...
rows.statement: Implements Step 279's rule-combination algebra as executable code: a precedence list [DENY, CONFLICT, CONDITIONAL, UNKNOWN, PASS] and a Combine() function that scans results in exactly that precedence order, unioning required/satisfied/missing condition sets across multiple CONDITIONAL results and preferring a BLOCK resolution strategy when present among them; falls through to PASS only if all results are PASS, otherwise INDETERMINATE.
invariants: DENY > CONFLICT > CONDITIONAL > UNKNOWN > PASS precedence

rows.anchor: def __post_init__(self): if self.authority is None: raise PolicyError("missing authority") ... if not self.scope: raise PolicyError("inconsistent scope: empty") ids=[r.id for r in self.rules] if len(ids)!=len(set(ids)): raise PolicyError("invalid rules: duplicate rule id") @property def PID(self) -> str: ... return hashlib.sha256(c.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
rows.statement: Implements the Policy schema's rejection invariants as an executable __post_init__ validator (raising PolicyError for missing authority, malformed validity interval, empty scope, or duplicate rule ids), and implements the content-addressed policy identity PID as a truncated SHA-256 hash over a canonical JSON serialization of id/version/rule-ids/parameters/authority/validity/scope.

rows.anchor: ok=[a for a in active if o.scope<=a.scope and o.jurisdiction<=a.jurisdiction] bad=[a for a in active if a not in ok] if ok and bad: # F4: conflicting determinations if precedence: ... return Verdict(DENY,"AuthorityConflict") if not ok: return Verdict(DENY,"ScopeOrJurisdictionExceeded") return Verdict(PASS,f"Permit:{ok[0].id}")
rows.statement: Implements the Authorize() function realizing the scope/jurisdiction subset invariant (Permit requires operation scope and jurisdiction to be subsets of the authority's), fail-closed defaults (no authorities -> DENY 'NoAuthority'; none active at time t -> DENY 'NoAuthority'; scope/jurisdiction exceeded -> DENY), and a conflicting-determinations branch (F4) that either applies a precedence tiebreak or returns DENY 'AuthorityConflict' when no precedence is declared -- never silently defaulting to Permit.

type_signature.domain: list of Authority, an Operation, optional Policy, time t, optional precedence map

invariants: Permit implies Scope(o) subseteq Scope(a) and Jurisdiction(o) subseteq Jurisdiction(a)

rows.anchor: class PolicyStore: def __init__(self): self._h:List[Policy]=[]; ... def activate(self,pi:Policy): for p in self._h: if p.PID==pi.PID: raise PolicyError("duplicate version identity") ... def PolicyAt(self,t:str)->Verdict: c=[p for p in self._h if Applicable(p,t)] if not c: return Verdict(UNKNOWN,"NoApplicablePolicy") if len(c)>1: return Verdict(CONFLICT,"OverlappingPolicies:"+...) return Verdict(PASS,c[0].version)
rows.statement: Implements the historical PolicyStore: activate() rejects duplicate version identity (PID collisions), history() returns the full immutable list (never overwritten), and PolicyAt(t) returns UNKNOWN 'NoApplicablePolicy' when no policy is applicable at t, CONFLICT 'OverlappingPolicies:...' when more than one applies, or PASS with the single applicable version otherwise -- realizing the never-silently-select-a-policy requirement from Step 279 §15.
invariants: no two activated policies may share a PID
PolicyAt never silently selects among overlapping applicable policies

rows.anchor: # F8 unauthorized policy mutation try: POL.rules=(mk("rX",DENY),); mutated=True except Exception as ex: mutated=False; exmsg=type(ex).__name__ T("F8","Unauthorized policy mutation","Deny; active policy unchanged", ..., (not mutated) and [r.id for r in store.history()[0].rules]==["r1"],4)
rows.statement: F8 (unauthorized policy mutation) is executed by directly attempting to reassign the .rules attribute on an already-created Policy object; the Python frozen-dataclass mechanism itself raises an exception, blocking the mutation, and the harness verifies both that the mutation raised and that the policy's stored rules in the PolicyStore remain unchanged, confirming the active-policy-immutability invariant holds at the implementation level.

experiment.hypothesis: An unauthorized/direct attempt to mutate an active Policy object's rules should fail, leaving the stored policy unchanged.
experiment.setup: An already-activated Policy object in a PolicyStore.
experiment.assumptions: Python's frozen dataclass mechanism enforces immutability strictly enough to stand in for a domain-level immutability invariant.
experiment.inputs: A direct attribute-reassignment attempt on POL.rules.
experiment.method: Attempt the reassignment inside a try/except and check both whether an exception was raised and whether the store's copy of the policy's rules is unchanged.
experiment.result: The mutation attempt raised an exception, and the stored policy's rules remained ['r1'].

sources.note: A ~3000-line rigorous mathematical rewrite of the consolidated KnowledgeOS theory strictly separating definitions/theorems/empirical-findings/conjectures/heuristics. Proves Theorem 1 (H(Q|R)=0 iff Q almost-surely a deterministic function of R), Theorem 2 (conditional-entropy monotonicity under deterministic reduction via the data-processing inequality), and Theorem 3 (adequacy equivalent to Q-homogeneity of representation fibers), all with full proofs. Introduces no-excess/sufficiency-vs-minimality, Q-equivalence-vs-Q-isomorphism, fiber-collision preservation-boundary characterization, a homomorphic-defect formalization, a four-level statistical-generalization hierarchy, a seven-element meta-structure K=(D,R,T,Q,Pi,E,O), explicit algebra-readiness criteria (closure/associativity/identity/inverse), and a final three-equation unification for adequacy/Zero/realization. Recommends next building a formal theorem/lemma/conjecture register with nine classification tags.

rows.statement: States the governing improvement of this pass over the prior consolidated draft: strictly distinguish definitions, proven mathematical propositions/theorems, empirical findings, conjectures, and research heuristics, since some equations previously presented as empirical results are actually mathematical consequences of the definitions under explicit assumptions.

lineage_claims.quote: There is an important improvement I would make to the previous version

rows.anchor: Theorem 1 -- Functional recoverability criterion. Let D be a random variable, R=T(D), and Q=Q(D) ... H(Q|R)=0 if and only if Q is almost surely a deterministic function of R. Proof: H(Q|R) = sum_r P(R=r) H(Q|R=r) ... Q=g(R) almost surely.
rows.statement: Proves Theorem 1 (functional recoverability criterion): for discrete finite-valued random variables, H(Q|R)=0 if and only if Q is almost surely a deterministic function of R, with a complete proof via the decomposition H(Q|R)=sum_r P(R=r)H(Q|R=r) and the observation that each conditional distribution with positive probability must be degenerate.

rows.anchor: N_viol=0 => empirical adequacy on the tested sample. This does not imply population adequacy. That distinction is fundamental.
rows.statement: Formalizes the finite-sample operational adequacy criterion: a deterministic empirical decoder exists iff every representation value corresponds to at most one inquiry value in the test set (equivalently N_viol=0), which implies only empirical adequacy on the tested sample, never population adequacy.

rows.anchor: H(R) = H(Q) + H(R|Q) - H(Q|R) ... If the representation is adequate, H(Q|R)=0. Therefore H(R)=H(Q)+H(R|Q). Hence H(R)>=H(Q). Equality occurs iff H(R|Q)=0. Therefore H(R)=H(Q) iff H(Q|R)=0 and H(R|Q)=0.
rows.statement: Derives the general chain-rule identity H(R)=H(Q)+H(R|Q)-H(Q|R), specializing under adequacy (H(Q|R)=0) to H(R)=H(Q)+H(R|Q), hence H(R)>=H(Q) with equality iff H(R|Q)=0 as well -- the mathematically precise form of the earlier informal 'no representational excess' idea.

rows.anchor: NoExcess(R,Q) iff H(R|Q)=0. ... Adequacy: H(Q|R)=0. No excess: H(R|Q)=0. These are logically independent conditions in general. ... Adequate with excess: H(Q|R)=0, H(R|Q)>0. Inadequate: H(Q|R)>0. ... Sufficiency != Minimality.
rows.statement: Defines NoExcess(R,Q) iff H(R|Q)=0 and formally establishes that adequacy (H(Q|R)=0) and no-excess (H(R|Q)=0) are logically independent conditions in general -- a representation can be 'adequate with excess' (H(Q|R)=0 but H(R|Q)>0) or inadequate (H(Q|R)>0) -- yielding the new distinction Sufficiency != Minimality.

rows.anchor: R1 ~_Q R2 when Q(decode(R1)) = Q(decode(R2)). However, the theory should not call this Q-isomorphism. ... equality of inquiry outcomes does not establish structural isomorphism. Q-equivalent != Q-isomorphic. The latter requires additional structural conditions.
rows.statement: Defines Q-equivalence between representations (R1 ~_Q R2 iff Q(decode(R1))=Q(decode(R2))) and explicitly distinguishes it from 'Q-isomorphism', since equality of inquiry outcomes does not establish structural isomorphism, which requires additional structural conditions not implied by Q-equivalence alone.

rows.anchor: Theorem 2 -- Conditional entropy monotonicity under deterministic reduction. Let Q -> R_n -> R_{n-1} form a Markov chain, with R_{n-1}=T_n(R_n) deterministically. Then H(Q|R_{n-1}) >= H(Q|R_n). Proof: data-processing inequality gives I(Q;R_{n-1}) <= I(Q;R_n) ... cancel H(Q) ... QED.
rows.statement: Proves Theorem 2 (conditional entropy monotonicity under deterministic reduction): for a Markov chain Q->R_n->R_{n-1} with R_{n-1}=T_n(R_n) deterministic, H(Q|R_{n-1})>=H(Q|R_n), derived rigorously from the data-processing inequality I(Q;R_{n-1})<=I(Q;R_n) via I(Q;R)=H(Q)-H(Q|R); the corollary chain H(Q|R5)<=H(Q|R4)<=H(Q|R3)<=H(Q|R2) shows information sufficiency cannot spontaneously reappear once lost.

lineage_claims.quote: once information sufficiency has been lost in a deterministic chain, it cannot spontaneously reappear. This is a mathematical theorem, not an empirical discovery

rows.anchor: A_n = 1{H(Q|R_n)=0}. Then, under exact population adequacy and deterministic degradation: A_n=1 => A_{n-1}<=A_n. Equivalently, adequacy can transition 1->0 but cannot transition 0->1. Thus a preservation boundary can be defined as the first transition: R_k adequate, R_{k-1} inadequate.
rows.statement: Formalizes the preservation boundary using an adequacy indicator A_n=1{H(Q|R_n)=0}: under deterministic sequential degradation, adequacy can only transition from 1 to 0, never from 0 to 1, so the preservation boundary is precisely defined as the first transition point R_k adequate, R_{k-1} inadequate.

rows.anchor: min_{T in T} C(T(D)) subject to H(Q(D)|T(D))=0. ... C(R) = w1 bytes(R) + w2 latency(R) + w3 storage(R) + ... but the weights must be business-defined. Reduction is an optimization problem subject to preservation.
rows.statement: Formalizes reduction as a constrained optimization problem: minimize a business-defined representation-cost functional C(T(D)) (e.g. weighted bytes, latency, storage) subject to the adequacy constraint H(Q(D)|T(D))=0, explicitly marked as a candidate mathematical formulation, not yet an established KnowledgeOS law.

A representational convention can carry operational consequences. But the pure 'decoder-only effect' attribution was to
rows.statement: Records the formal audit correction that the ascending/descending rank transformations were not proven to be simple invertible recodings, since deterministic tie-breaking on data with repeated values (e.g. D=[23000,46000,46000]) makes desc != (n+1)-asc; the broader lesson survives (a representational convention can carry operational consequences) but the pure 'decoder-only effect' attribution was too strong and had to be corrected after audit.

If this equality fails, define the defect: Delta_f(a,b) = f(a otimes_A b) - f(a) otimes_B f(b) only when an appropriate difference operation exists. Otherwise define a typed defect relation: Def_f(a,b). The theory must not assume homomorphism. It
rows.statement: Formalizes the homomorphic-defect quantity for structure-preserving transformations: when f(a otimes_A b) != f(a) otimes_B f(b), define Delta_f(a,b)=f(a otimes_A b) - f(a) otimes_B f(b) if a difference operation exists in the target space, otherwise a typed defect relation Def_f(a,b) when it does not, establishing that homomorphism must be measured, never assumed.

rows.anchor: A specific decoder is: O: R -> Y. Realization requires: O(R) = Q(D). A representation can therefore contain sufficient information while a particular decoder fails to recover it. Adequacy != Realization. ... Decoder theorem: if Q is recoverable from R, then there exists an ideal decoder g* such that
rows.statement: Proves the decoder theorem: if Q is recoverable from R there exists an ideal decoder g* with g*(R)=Q, but an arbitrary decoder O need not equal g*, so H(Q|R)=0 does not imply O(R)=Q without additional conditions on O -- formally separating representation sufficiency (adequacy) from implementation realization.

rows.anchor: Q(D1)=Q(D2) ... This relation IS an equivalence relation because equality is reflexive, symmetric, transitive. Therefore Q partitions the source space: D/~_Q. A representation T is adequate for Q precisely when it distinguishes enough classes to recover the Q-class. Q(D1)!=Q(D2) => T(D1)!=T(D2).
rows.statement: Establishes that the relation D1~D2 iff Q(D1)=Q(D2) is a genuine equivalence relation (equality being reflexive, symmetric, transitive), partitioning the source space into D/~_Q classes, with T adequate for Q precisely when it distinguishes enough classes to recover the Q-class, equivalently Q(D1)!=Q(D2) implies T(D1)!=T(D2).

rows.anchor: Theorem 3. For deterministic T, the following are equivalent on a domain D0: 1. H(Q|T(D))=0. 2. There exists g such that Q=g.T. 3. Whenever T(D1)=T(D2), then Q(D1)=Q(D2). Proof: 1<=>2 follows from Theorem 1. 2=>3 ... 3=>2: define g(r)=Q(D) for any D with T(D)=r; well-defined by condition 3. QED. Thi
rows.statement: Proves Theorem 3, establishing the equivalence, for deterministic T, of (1) H(Q|T(D))=0, (2) existence of g with Q=g.T, and (3) T(D1)=T(D2) implies Q(D1)=Q(D2), with a complete proof; judged extremely useful for KnowledgeOS because it converts semantic preservation into a concrete fiber-separation condition.

rows.anchor: T^{-1}(r) = {D: T(D)=r}. Adequacy means: Q is constant on every fiber of T. ... Representation reduction is safe iff every representation fiber is Q-homogeneous.
rows.statement: Defines the fiber T^{-1}(r)={D:T(D)=r} of a representation and characterizes adequacy as Q being constant on every fiber of T, giving the clean formulation that representation reduction is safe if and only if every representation fiber is Q-homogeneous -- judged a stronger conceptual formulation than merely 'information was preserved'.

rows.anchor: A reduction transformation T1 -> T2 crosses a preservation boundary precisely when T2 creates at least one Q-heterogeneous fiber: exists D1,D2: T2(D1)=T2(D2) but Q(D1)!=Q(D2). Boundary iff first occurrence of a Q-heterogeneous representation fiber. This gives a very concrete mathematical interpretat
rows.statement: Characterizes a preservation-boundary crossing as the first occurrence of a Q-heterogeneous representation fiber (T2 collapsing two source states D1,D2 with T2(D1)=T2(D2) but Q(D1)!=Q(D2)), giving a concrete mathematical interpretation of the experimental N_viol statistic as counting such fiber collisions.

rows.anchor: Hhat(Q|R)=0 does not establish H(Q|R)=0 in the population. It establishes only a sample-level result under the estimator and observed support. Hhat=0 !=> H=0 without additional statistical assumptions. This distinction is mandatory.
rows.statement: Mandates the population-vs-sample distinction as a formal requirement: the empirical estimator result Hhat(Q|R)=0 establishes only a sample-level result under the given estimator and observed support, never the population-level H(Q|R)=0, without additional statistical assumptions.

rows.statement: Details the specific audit finding that a proposed bootstrap confidence interval for conditional entropy was invalid because sparse resampling changed the support structure, listing six required remedial steps (define estimator, establish assumptions, evaluate finite-sample bias, apply corrections, validate bootstrap conditions, distinguish empirical from population support), while noting the main preservation conclusion survived since it rested on exact violation counts and train/test agreement rather than the invalid confidence interval.

rows.anchor: Level 1 -- Observed: Hhat(Q|R) or N_viol. Level 2 -- Experimental conclusion: within the tested sample and design, preservation was/was not observed. Level 3 -- Statistical generalization: requires sampling assumptions, estimator validity, uncertainty quantification, population model. Level 4 -- Mat
rows.statement: Establishes a formal four-level statistical-generalization hierarchy that must never be collapsed: Level 1 Observed (Hhat(Q|R) or N_viol), Level 2 Experimental conclusion (within the tested sample/design), Level 3 Statistical generalization (requiring sampling assumptions, estimator validity, uncertainty quantification, population model), Level 4 Mathematical theorem (requiring proof).

rows.statement: Specifies the concrete algebraic properties (closure, associativity, identity, inverse) that would need to be proved, not assumed, for any candidate carrier (X,+,*) to be legitimately called an algebra, explicitly warning against assuming any of these merely because a transformation produces something informally labeled 'Zero'; concludes the project currently has a transformation theory but not yet a proven Knowledge Algebra.

rows.statement: Unifies the entire theory into three commutation/recoverability equations -- Q=g.T (adequacy), Pi.T=Pi.T.E_S (Zero), Q=O.T (realization) -- with g establishing adequacy, E_S establishing Zero/eliminability, and O establishing realization, judged the most mathematically elegant form of the theory developed so far.

Transformation-relative Zero is a
rows.statement: States the final consolidated theory paragraph for this pass, summarizing purpose-relative transformation, the formal adequacy criterion H(Q|R)=0 equivalently Q=g.T, the sequential monotonicity theorem, Transformation-relative Zero as a non-algebraic counterfactual eliminability predicate that is neither necessary nor sufficient for preservation, and the explicit absence of any universal carrier, algebra, reduction law, or extraction calculus.

rows.statement: A 5-category contradiction classification is proposed to prevent incorrectly 'resolving' harmless historical variation: C1 genuine logical contradiction, C2 competing models (no equivalence proof), C3 refinement, C4 projection/view difference, C5 terminological/type collision.

aliases: Business meaning: safe removal vs outcome preservation

sources.note: A three-part business-language translation of the KR-ZERO/KR-REP-REDUCTION/KR-BRIDGE-01 research: introduces a customer-record example distinguishing Zero (unnecessary for a given purpose) from universal uselessness; a five-step governed transformation architecture (identify business question, define required outcome, transform, verify preservation, separately test removability); a list of claims not yet supportable to management; and a refined three-way business distinction Removability != Preservation != Realization mapped to Zero/eliminability, adequacy/recoverability, and decoder/realization research respectively. Notably self-corrects a provenance error (misattributing the BRIDGE-01 redundancy-confounding finding to the KR-REP-REDUCTION assessment) and reconciles the two experiments as complementary, not merged, evidence strands.

rows.anchor: We have evidence that 'information can be removed safely' and 'information can be removed without changing the business outcome' are two different questions.
rows.statement: States the business meaning of the research in one sentence: there is evidence that 'information can be removed safely' and 'information can be removed without changing the business outcome' are two different questions, a distinction argued to be useful for KnowledgeOS.

rows.anchor: Customer = Muller, Order = EUR1,000, Sales channel = Online, Timestamp = 10:42 ... 'Which sales channel generated the highest revenue?' ... the timestamp might be unnecessary. ... Zero is not 'useless information.' It is 'information that is unnecessary for this particular business purpose.'
rows.statement: Illustrates Zero with a customer-record business example: a timestamp can be removed without changing the answer to 'which sales channel generated the highest revenue' but may be essential for 'which order happened first', establishing that Zero means information unnecessary for a particular business purpose, not universally useless information.

rows.anchor: The experiment tested whether this 'removability' concept is automatically connected to preservation of the business result. The answer was: No -- not in the tested setup. ... Business decision A: 'Can I remove this information?' and Business decision B: 'Will the business result remain correct?' mu
rows.statement: Translates the bridge experiment's negative result into business terms: whether information is removable ('business decision A') and whether the business result remains correct ('business decision B') must be treated as separate governance questions, since a rule of the form 'IF Zero=true THEN information may safely be discarded' is not supported by the evidence.

rows.anchor: Important for what? Under which transformation? For which business question? ... Timestamp / Total revenue / Possibly. Timestamp / Order sequence / No. Customer ID / Revenue by channel / Possibly. Customer ID / Customer history / No. Duplicate transaction / Total unique customers / Maybe. Duplicate
rows.statement: Proposes that KnowledgeOS reason about information relevance relative to a purpose rather than treating relevance as absolute, illustrated with a six-row example table (timestamp/customer-ID/duplicate-transaction against different business questions with different removability answers) instead of the naive binary 'important or unimportant' framing.

rows.anchor: Initially, the experiment showed an apparent relationship: More Zero -> less preservation. ... when the experiment controlled for redundancy/duplication, that relationship disappeared ... We initially thought two things were related, but a third factor was influencing both. ... Sales dropped after a
rows.statement: Translates the bridge experiment's confounding discovery into a familiar business-analysis pattern using a CRM/sales-drop example (a correlation between a new CRM and falling sales does not establish causation if a market downturn coincided), arguing this is exactly the kind of discipline the redundancy-controlled experiment demonstrated.

rows.anchor: Step 1 -- Identify the business question. Step 2 -- Define the required business outcome. Step 3 -- Transform the representation. Step 4 -- Verify preservation. Step 5 -- Separately test removability. That separation is potentially a KnowledgeOS architectural principle.
rows.statement: Proposes a five-step safer architecture for AI-driven information reduction -- identify the business question, define the required business outcome, transform the representation, verify preservation, and separately test removability -- as a candidate KnowledgeOS architectural principle, contrasted with the dangerous naive approach of deleting information merely because it looks redundant.

rows.anchor: We should not currently tell the business: 'We have invented a universal Knowledge Algebra.' ... 'Zero means safe deletion.' Not established. And not: 'Zero predicts preservation.' The experiment specifically did not support that. And not: 'We have found the fundamental information unit.' The carrie
rows.statement: Lists four claims that must not currently be made to the business: that a universal Knowledge Algebra has been invented, that Zero means safe deletion, that Zero predicts preservation (specifically unsupported by the experiment), and that the fundamental information unit/carrier has been found (it remains open).

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS = system that finds unnecessary information and removes it. ... I think the research is pushing us toward something more powerful: KnowledgeOS = system that determines what information can be transformed or removed while preserving a specified business meaning. ... The core is: purpose-p
rows.statement: Revises the KnowledgeOS vision from 'a system that finds and removes unnecessary information' to 'a system that determines what information can be transformed or removed while preserving a specified business meaning', naming purpose-preserving transformation of information as the core, and mapping this onto the four-layer Representation -> Transformation -> Observation -> Preservation separation in business language (how is information represented, what are we changing, what business result are we looking at, what must remain true).

rows.anchor: Can information sometimes be removed without changing a defined outcome? Yes, demonstrated. Is removability the same as preservation? No evidence; BRIDGE points against treating them as equivalent. ... Do we have a universal reduction law? No. Do we have a universal 'Zero' law? No. ... So I would no
rows.statement: Produces an eight-row strategic status table (removability demonstrated, removability!=preservation per BRIDGE, redundancy affects both in the tested regime, misleading correlations detectable, no universal reduction/Zero law, carrier unknown, promising research direction exists), concluding this should not be called a failure but a move from 'maybe Zero and preservation are one thing' to experimental evidence that they are separate dimensions whose apparent relationship can be caused by structural factors like redundancy.

rows.anchor: The attached file I actually reviewed is the KR-REP-REDUCTION assessment, and it does not contain the 'BRIDGE-01' result or the specific claim that redundancy caused the apparent Zero/preservation relationship to disappear. The attached assessment instead reports that Zero did not correlate with the
rows.statement: Catches and corrects a provenance error: the file actually under review was the KR-REP-REDUCTION assessment, which does not contain the BRIDGE-01 redundancy-confounding result; that assessment only reports that Zero did not correlate with the observed preservation boundary in the representation-reduction experiment, so the redundancy/BRIDGE conclusion must not be attributed to this particular file.

rows.anchor: Information is not simply 'important' or 'unimportant.' Its removability and its preservation value must be evaluated relative to the business question and the required outcome. ... Zero(x|Q1) != Zero(x|Q2) is a much better conceptual representation than Zero(x). ... we should not yet turn that into
rows.statement: Reformulates the clean business statement actually supported by the KR-REP-REDUCTION assessment: information is not simply important or unimportant, its removability and preservation value must be evaluated relative to the business question and required outcome, represented as Zero(x|Q1) != Zero(x|Q2) rather than the unqualified Zero(x), explicitly marked as a candidate interpretation consistent with the broader Zero research rather than a universal formal law.

rows.anchor: 1. Removability: Can this information be eliminated under the current context and transformation? Zero / eliminability research. 2. Preservation: Does the resulting representation still preserve what the business inquiry requires? Adequacy / recoverability research. 3. Realization: Can the designate
rows.statement: Formulates the emerging KnowledgeOS business model as three distinct questions rather than two -- Removability (Zero/eliminability research), Preservation (adequacy/recoverability research), and Realization (decoder/realization research) -- summarized as Removability != Preservation != Realization, noting the KR-REP-REDUCTION experiment gives particularly strong support to the Preservation-vs-Realization separation specifically.

rows.anchor: 'We compress your information.' The stronger KnowledgeOS story is: 'We transform your information while explicitly defining what business meaning must survive the transformation.' ... Not min Size(R) but something closer to min Cost(R) subject to Adequate(R,Q,Pi). And the experiment has already demo
rows.statement: Contrasts a naive AI compression story ('we compress your information') with a stronger commercial KnowledgeOS story ('we transform your information while explicitly defining what business meaning must survive'), reformulating the optimization target from minimizing representation size to minimizing cost subject to an explicit adequacy constraint Adequate(R,Q,Pi), motivated by the experiment's demonstration that the first representation-reduction step can already cross a preservation boundary.

rows.anchor: The measured reduction dimensions behave differently: bytes, fields, cardinality, entropy. The assessment therefore rejects collapsing reduction into one simple scalar. ... 'Reduce the data by 80%.' But KnowledgeOS should ask: 80% of what? 80% fewer bytes? 80% fewer records? 80% fewer semantic claim
rows.statement: Argues compression alone should not be the commercial objective since the measured reduction dimensions (bytes, fields, cardinality, entropy) behave differently and cannot be collapsed into one scalar, illustrated with a business request to 'reduce the data by 80%' which is ambiguous across at least five genuinely different objectives (bytes, records, semantic claims, entropy, business-relevant distinctions).

rows.anchor: The assessment explicitly found no demonstrated relationship between Zero and the observed preservation boundary. Therefore the architecture should not be: Zero = true -> SAFE DELETE. Instead: Business Inquiry Q -> Preservation Contract Pi -> Candidate Transformation -> Zero / Adequacy -> Decision.
rows.statement: Warns against an architecture of the form 'Zero=true implies SAFE DELETE', proposing instead a flow where a business inquiry Q and preservation contract Pi govern a candidate transformation whose Zero (removability) and Adequacy (preservation) outcomes are evaluated independently before a decision, with decoder realization kept as a further independent concern.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS research is investigating whether information can be transformed or removed while preserving a defined business meaning. Initial experiments show that removability, preservation, and realization are distinct concerns. ... if the separate BRIDGE-01 experiment has independently established
rows.statement: Drafts recommended management wording (removability, preservation, and realization are distinct concerns supported by initial experiments) and insists that any redundancy/BRIDGE-01 finding be kept as a separate evidence strand, addable only after the actual BRIDGE-01 artifact itself is reviewed, rather than folded into the KR-REP-REDUCTION-based statement.

rationale_evidence.statement: Translates the bridge experiment's confounding discovery into a familiar business-analysis pattern using a CRM/sales-drop example (a correlation between a new CRM and falling sales does not establish causation if a market downturn coincided), arguing this is exactly the kind of discipline the redundancy-controlled experiment demonstrated.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Can information sometimes be removed without changing a defined outcome? Yes, demonstrated. Is removability the same as preservation? rationale_evidence.statement: Produces an eight-row strategic status table (removability demonstrated, removability!=preservation per BRIDGE, redundancy affects both in the tested regime, misleading correlations detectable, no universal reduction/Zero law, carrier unknown, promising research direction exists), concluding this should not be called a failure but a move from 'maybe Zero and preservation are one thing' to experimental evidence that they are separate dimensions whose apparent relationship can be caused by structural factors like redundancy.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 'We compress your information.' rationale_evidence.statement: Contrasts a naive AI compression story ('we compress your information') with a stronger commercial KnowledgeOS story ('we transform your information while explicitly defining what business meaning must survive'), reformulating the optimization target from minimizing representation size to minimizing cost subject to an explicit adequacy constraint Adequate(R,Q,Pi), motivated by the experiment's demonstration that the first representation-reduction step can already cross a preservation boundary.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The measured reduction dimensions behave differently: bytes, fields, cardinality, entropy. The assessment therefore rejects collapsing reduction into one simple scalar. ... rationale_evidence.statement: Argues compression alone should not be the commercial objective since the measured reduction dimensions (bytes, fields, cardinality, entropy) behave differently and cannot be collapsed into one scalar, illustrated with a business request to 'reduce the data by 80%' which is ambiguous across at least five genuinely different objectives (bytes, records, semantic claims, entropy, business-relevant distinctions).

sources.note: The adopted invariant that a governance-evidence conflict must never be resolved by silently choosing a side, deleting history, or rewriting sequence; operationalized via STRICT EXTENSION vs PREFIX DISAGREEMENT tests and later a CASE alpha/beta pre-switch/post-switch split.

rows.anchor: R-CONFLICT (PROPOSED): a conflict in the authority record is never resolved by choosing a side. seq density (O-6) makes loss detectable; a resolution that leaves a seq gap is invalid by construction.
rows.statement: Proposes R-CONFLICT: any resolution of a governance-evidence conflict is invalid by construction if it leaves a sequence gap, chooses one side silently, or is otherwise not seq-density-preserving.
missing: operational mechanics — supplied later by the implementation design

rows.anchor: History ≠ Reconstruction Guess
rows.statement: A candidate governance principle proposed alongside R-CONFLICT and other estate principles (Recording ≠ Asserting; Reference ≠ Ownership): History ≠ Reconstruction Guess — recorded as a recommendation, not yet adopted at this point in the file.

rows.anchor: D2 constrains how D1 is implemented — this is the load-bearing consequence.
rows.statement: The R-CONFLICT decision (D2) binds how the relocation (D1) may be implemented: the migration must preserve sequence integrity and provenance, must not delete or re-create history, and if a relocated record and a runtime record ever diverge, R-CONFLICT governs — neither side may be silently chosen.

rows.anchor: STRICT EXTENSION ... append the runtime tail M+1…N ... PREFIX DISAGREEMENT ... MUST NOT be resolved mechanically.
rows.statement: R-CONFLICT is operationalized into exactly two mechanically-distinguishable divergence shapes: STRICT EXTENSION (the common prefix is byte-identical and one side merely extends further — resolved automatically as a union, not a choice) and PREFIX DISAGREEMENT (the common prefix itself differs — a genuine authority conflict that must be recorded, preserved on both sides, and escalated to a PO/ARB act, never resolved mechanically).

rows.anchor: RC-9 — 'canonical re-encode' is not defined ... a false CASE B (escalation) rather than a false CASE A (silent merge) — the safe direction
rows.statement: RC-9: the plan's 'common prefix byte-identical' comparison rule for CASE A does not define its canonicalization method (e.g. key-order sorting), and since JSON decode/encode preserves insertion order, two semantically equal but differently-ordered records would compare unequal, producing a false escalation to CASE B rather than a false silent merge (CASE A) — the safe failure direction, but ambiguous as written.

rows.anchor: RD-3 — Phase-7 mismatch disposition routes post-demotion writes into §6 CASE A, which would import non-authoritative bytes that §8 says require a governance act
rows.statement: RD-3: AMD4 routes every Phase-7 mismatch to the same reconciliation logic (CASE A/B), but CASE A appends the runtime tail as a legitimate extension, meaning a post-writer-switch write to the demoted store would be silently imported into the authoritative store — contradicting the plan's own rule that re-promoting a demoted source is a governance act, not a merge.

rows.anchor: CASE α — pre-writer-switch ... RECONCILE under §6 ... CASE β — post-writer-switch ... not authoritative — written against a demoted store ... QUARANTINE · record the conflict · ESCALATE. Never imported.
rows.statement: AMD5 splits the Phase-7 mismatch disposition into two named cases with opposite treatment: CASE α (pre-writer-switch, authoritatively-produced bytes) reconciles under the existing R-CONFLICT logic, while CASE β (post-writer-switch, written against an already-demoted store) is quarantined, recorded as a conflict, and escalated — never imported — with a conservative tie-break (unresolvable ordering defaults to CASE β).
missing: a terminating condition for CASE β — later found missing by the AMD5 review

rows.anchor: RD-3·a — CASE β has no terminating condition, and criteria 12 and 15 are jointly unsatisfiable in it ... after a β event the runtime source therefore never equals manifest + reconciled delta, so §4.4's own gate can never be satisfied
rows.statement: Two of AMD5's own acceptance criteria are jointly unsatisfiable after a CASE β event: criterion 12 requires the runtime source to equal 'manifest + reconciled delta' before removal, but criterion 15 defines CASE β bytes as deliberately never reconciled, so the removal gate could never be satisfied, be permanently blocked, or be satisfied only by destroying the quarantined bytes — none of which the plan states.
missing: a stated terminating condition — the residual this finding identifies

rows.anchor: The conflict history becomes a domain event stream rather than simply an overwritten database row. That gives KnowledgeOS much stronger reconstruction capability.
rows.statement: Reframes the R-CONFLICT concept as an event stream (EvidenceQualified events from two sources triggering EvidenceConflictDetected, then Conflict Resolution, then ConflictResolved), arguing this gives much stronger reconstruction capability than treating the conflict as an overwritten database row.

rows.anchor: EvidenceConflict ... - ConflictId - ConflictingEvidence[] - DetectedAt - ConflictType - ResolutionStatus - ResolutionAuthority - ResolutionDecision ... A conflict resolution must preserve: provenance; history; reconstruction capability.
rows.statement: Models the R-CONFLICT idea as a first-class EvidenceConflict domain aggregate (with ConflictId, ConflictingEvidence[], DetectedAt, ConflictType, ResolutionStatus, ResolutionAuthority, ResolutionDecision fields), owned by the Knowledge Evidence Context, whose invariant requires any resolution to preserve provenance, history, and reconstruction capability.
invariants: A conflict resolution must preserve provenance, history, reconstruction capability.

rows.anchor: RECORD EXISTENCE != AUTHORITY ESTABLISHMENT; PHYSICAL STORAGE ORDER != DOMAIN EVENT ORDER
rows.statement: Two DDD non-confusions asserted as load-bearing for the migration's DV-3 correction: the durable store may already contain copied governance records before authority transfers, and those copied records do not themselves establish authority; the authority-boundary discriminator must be the domain event (the transfer), never physical file position.

rows.anchor: A self-check that can assert its own success is EVIDENCE, never assurance.
rows.statement: The assurance-tooling boundary discipline: an author's own trace/test suite is required delivered evidence but never discharges the independent-review gate.

rows.anchor: QUARANTINE LAUNDERING: moving a post-demotion record out of the demoted store would hide the quarantined evidence, making the source spuriously satisfy the final-rehash comparison and incorrectly opening the removal branch.
rows.statement: Names and corrects an inverted rationale (the original plan said a move would 'break the enumeration'; the corrected reasoning is the opposite -- a move makes a comparison PASS when it should FAIL) -- a general anti-pattern for any evidence-quarantine mechanism.

lineage_claims.quote: the inverted reason is withdrawn, not softened... it is false in the direction that matters

rows.anchor: PREMISE 2: a migration mechanical write on a store confers no authority, and is evidenced by a governance append that describes it -- which is what makes the placement-decision recursion terminate.
rows.statement: The load-bearing premise of the C-4 termination argument, moved inside the argument by this correction; without it the argument for where evidence lands would appear to terminate after one iteration when it does not.

rows.anchor: 23 of 30 concurrent-append trials silently lost a transition; every survivor was dense and monotonic -- density is NOT a completeness proof.
rows.statement: A reproduced concurrency experiment (mktemp dirs via --dir, never against the live corpus) showing the read-modify-write append path has no lock/lease/CAS, so a losing writer's transaction vanishes while the surviving sequence remains perfectly dense -- refuting an earlier absolute 'no record silently dropped' claim.

experiment.hypothesis: the append path's atomic rename makes concurrent appends safe
experiment.setup: mktemp scratch directories via --dir, concurrent-append trials against workflow-state.php
experiment.assumptions: no lock/lease/CAS exists (documented in the header)
experiment.inputs: 30 concurrent-append trials
experiment.method: technical Architecture review reproduced the race
experiment.result: 23/30 trials silently lost a transition; the losing process still exited 0 reporting success; every surviving sequence stayed dense and monotonic
experiment.interpretation: a dense, monotonic sequence number does not prove no record was lost, because the clobbering writer reuses the lost writer's sequence number
experiment.limitations: reproduced only in scratch directories, not against the production corpus
experiment.conclusion: the absolute completeness claim is withdrawn; only 'no record lost relative to the frozen manifest and observed inputs' is provable

rows.anchor: quarantine is a domain state with a business consequence, not a directory condition: an undisposed conflict means the migration aggregate cannot legitimately transition to its completed state.
rows.statement: A DDD reading of the quarantine mechanism: a single undisposed quarantine can block migration completion indefinitely, by design, because the aggregate refuses an invalid state transition rather than because of a tooling limitation.

rows.anchor: Removal (Phase 7) is not Deletion: evidence persists at the verified durable target, a byte-verified copy exists and is authoritative, history is relocated with provenance intact -- and removal occurs only after Phase 4 hash verification passed and Phase 5 switched.
rows.statement: Distinguishes the migration's terminal cleanup act from the R-CONFLICT-forbidden act of destroying historical governance evidence.

sources.note: Step 201's twenty-dimension review checklist (semantic integrity, ontological necessity, mathematical necessity, causal validity, temporal integrity, historical-vs-current state, epistemic integrity, uncertainty/authority/lineage preservation, counterfactual analysis, composition, boundary integrity, aggregate integrity, event integrity, idempotency, failure semantics, Unknown-as-first-class-result) plus a twelve-row concept review matrix, used to audit every accumulated architectural concept.

rows.anchor: | Concept | Mathematical role | DDD role | Governance role | Evidence role | Status |
rows.statement: Proposes a twelve-row review-instrument matrix (Identity, State, Transition, Evidence, Proposition, Assessment, Uncertainty, Authority, Decision, Action, Lineage, Invariant) crossing four role columns (mathematical, DDD, governance, evidence) with a review status column, explicitly not the final ontology but the review instrument to produce it.

rows.anchor: Does this word have exactly one meaning? ... State can mean: domain state; process state; epistemic state; infrastructure state; UI state.
rows.statement: Review dimension 1 (semantic integrity): challenges every term to have exactly one meaning, using 'State' as the running example of a word overloaded across at least five senses that must be split (DomainState, ProcessState, EpistemicState, etc.) where required.

rows.anchor: Is this actually an entity/concept in the domain, or merely an implementation artifact? ... DatabaseRecord does not automatically belong in the conceptual ontology. ... KafkaMessage does not automatically become a domain event.
rows.statement: Review dimension 2 (ontological necessity): distinguishes DomainConcept from TechnicalRepresentation, warning that neither a database record nor a message-bus message automatically qualifies as a domain concept or domain event.

rows.anchor: Mathematics must constrain the model, not decorate it.
rows.statement: Review dimension 3 (mathematical necessity): every introduced formula must actually constrain the architecture; forcing a probability P(x) onto every object merely because it sounds sophisticated is mathematically artificial and must be rejected.

rows.anchor: We must challenge every statement of the form: A\rightarrow B. Is this: causal? temporal? logical? probabilistic? merely correlated? merely sequential? ... Decision = f(Evidence,Policy,Authority,Context).
rows.statement: Review dimension 4 (causal validity): every arrow A->B in the architecture must be interrogated for whether it is causal, temporal, logical, probabilistic, correlational, or merely sequential -- e.g. Evidence->Decision should not be read as causation but as Decision=f(Evidence,Policy,Authority,Context).

rows.anchor: Truth(x,t) is often more accurate than: Truth(x). Likewise: Authority(a,d,t) rather than: Authority(a,d).
rows.statement: Review dimension 5 (temporal integrity): every important predicate should default to being time-indexed (Truth(x,t), Authority(a,d,t), Assessment(H,E,M,t)) rather than timeless.

rows.anchor: We need to test every aggregate against: CurrentState versus: HistoricalState. ... CurrentKnowledge \neq CompleteHistoricalKnowledge.
rows.statement: Review dimension 6 (historical vs current state): every aggregate must be tested to ensure its current-state projection does not accidentally destroy the ability to reconstruct governance-required history.

rows.anchor: Why do we believe this? ... We should reject: Claim\rightarrowTruth as an architectural shortcut. Instead: Claim \xrightarrow{assessment} EpistemicStatus.
rows.statement: Review dimension 7 (epistemic integrity): every knowledge claim must be traceable back to evidence or an explicitly declared assumption/model; Claim->Truth as a direct architectural shortcut is rejected in favor of Claim->assessment->EpistemicStatus.

rows.anchor: Does uncertainty remain visible? If it disappears without justification: Architecture defect ... Can we reconstruct why this actor was allowed to perform this transition at that point in time? If not: Governance defect ... If not, we have a traceability gap.
rows.statement: Review dimensions 8-10 (uncertainty, authority, and lineage preservation): deliberately trace constructed cases through Evidence->Assessment->Decision->Action and demand that uncertainty stay visible, authority remain reconstructible, and the full chain remain traceable backward from Outcome to Evidence -- any silent disappearance is labeled an architecture defect, governance defect, or traceability gap respectively.

rows.anchor: Y(A=1) versus: Y(A=0). This does not prove causality by itself, but it forces the architecture to distinguish: CausalClaim from: CorrelationClaim.
rows.statement: Review dimension 11 (counterfactual analysis): for every major causal claim, apply the potential-outcomes counterfactual frame Y(A=1) vs Y(A=0), which does not itself prove causation but forces a clean CausalClaim/CorrelationClaim distinction.

rows.anchor: Suppose P_1 is valid and: P_2 is valid. Does: P_1\circ P_2 remain valid? Not automatically. This becomes a major theme of the next phase.
rows.statement: Review dimension 12 (composition): restates and generalizes Step 198's composition-is-not-automatic result as an ongoing review discipline for the whole architecture.

rows.anchor: Which bounded context owns this meaning? We should be suspicious of concepts that appear everywhere. ... Decision may have different meanings in: Architecture Governance; Incident Management; Product Management; Compliance; Deployment.
rows.statement: Review dimension 13 (boundary integrity): every concept must have a clear owning bounded context; concepts appearing 'everywhere' (like Decision) should be suspected of hiding distinct domain semantics per context, even while sharing one mathematical abstraction.

rows.anchor: What invariant must this boundary protect? ... 'Because these objects belong together.' that is insufficient. The stronger answer is: 'They must change atomically because invariant I spans them.'
rows.statement: Review dimension 14 (aggregate integrity): restates the corpus's recurring DDD test for aggregate boundaries -- a shared-invariant justification is required, 'they belong together' is explicitly insufficient.

rows.anchor: Fact from: Command from: Decision from: Event. ... ApproveElection is a command. ... ElectionApproved is an event/fact.
rows.statement: Review dimension 15 (event integrity): distinguishes Fact, Command, Decision, and Event as four separate concepts, illustrated by ApproveElection (command) vs ElectionApproved (event/fact), warning that confusing them produces serious architectural ambiguity.

rows.anchor: If: \tau(x) is executed twice, what happens? We need to classify: \tau^2 as: equivalent; duplicate; invalid; compensating; state-changing.
rows.statement: Review dimension 16 (idempotency): every important transition must be tested against repeated execution and classified along five possible outcomes (equivalent, duplicate, invalid, compensating, state-changing), especially important for AI agents and distributed systems.

rows.anchor: TechnicalFailure ... BusinessRejection ... AuthorizationFailure ... ValidationFailure ... EpistemicInsufficiency ... Conflict. These are not interchangeable.
rows.statement: Review dimension 17 (failure semantics): a mature architecture must classify failure into distinct non-interchangeable categories (Technical, Business Rejection, Authorization, Validation, Epistemic Insufficiency, Conflict), not just describe Success.

rows.anchor: A system that has only: SUCCESS / FAILURE is probably hiding epistemic states. ... Unknown \rightarrow Retry? Unknown \rightarrow Escalation? Unknown \rightarrow DecisionWithRiskAcceptance? The answer is domain-specific.
rows.statement: Review dimension 18: a binary SUCCESS/FAILURE model likely hides epistemic states; Unknown must be deliberately tested as a first-class workflow result, with its handling (retry, escalation, or risk-accepted decision) determined by domain policy.
